paragraphs.text: OF OUR FATHER AMONG THE SAINTS, ARCHBISHOP OF CAESAREA IN CAPPADOCIA: REFUTATION OF THE APOLOGY OF THE IMPIOUS EUNOMIUS. I. If all those on whom the name of our God and Savior Jesus Christ has been invoked were willing to bring nothing new [?] into the [?] of the Gospel [?] of the impious Eunomius [?]

but to be content with the tradition of the apostles and the simplicity of the faith, we would have no need of words at present. Even now we would certainly have kept to the silence we embraced from the beginning. But the enemy of the truth always multiplies evil with fresh additions. Besides the tares he sowed in the Church of God from the beginning, he has now found instruments ready to receive his whole craft at once, and under the pretext of Christianity he brings in the denial of the divinity of the Only-begotten. With this vain wisdom from outside he throws into confusion the purity and simplicity of the teaching of the divine Spirit, and with plausible argument he leads the more simple-minded astray. So we too have been compelled, both for the sake of your love, since you laid this task on us, and for our own security, to set aside in this matter our [?]. Although we are wholly unpracticed in this kind of discourse, we have undertaken, according to the measure of knowledge supplied to us by the Lord, both to stand with the truth and to refute the falsehood. We reckoned that we could not fail to achieve at least one of three good results: either the refutation would provide a remedy for the evil to those already taken in, or it would offer a modest safeguard to those who are sound [?] In that book I did not read 'Refutation' (antirrhetikos) but 'Overthrow' (anatreptikos) [?] of the Apology of Eunomius. [?] Second Royal manuscript: 'Against Eunomius, Refutation' [?] of Saint Basil's refutations against Eunomius [?]

[?] has ever dared, preferring ambition to the good things allotted to the pious, he was emboldened to publish in this splendid treatise the blasphemy that until then had been muttered under the breath, eager to be proclaimed the leader and front-line champion of the whole heresy. It is he, then, whom we now propose to call to account. And since one and the same evil is in both, it is clear that in refuting the finished disciple we will also refute the teacher who sowed the seeds of impiety. May it be granted us, through your prayers, to receive such power of speech that, like the zealot Phinehas, we may strike both at once with a single blow of refutation, entwined with each other as they are in impiety. There are many ways in which I could show him in this treatise to be a liar, ignorant, insolent, a dissembler and a blasphemer. The rest I will mention only in passing; but the blasphemy he has uttered against the height of the glory of the Only-begotten I will try to strip of the coverings of his craft and make plain to all. 2. I will now proceed to the refutations, beginning from the title itself. First of all, the very form of his discourse is a piece of mischief he has devised, for he has composed his teaching in the guise of an apology, so that he may not seem to be setting out the doctrines of impiety on his own initiative, but to have been driven to these words by necessity. He wanted by every means to proclaim this wicked and godless message, and to bring into the open the blasphemy he had long ago conceived and labored with. But he saw that to take the teacher's chair openly would not only be very offensive and repugnant to his hearers, but would also make him unconvincing and suspect to the many, as a man who had turned to innovation out of a desire for glory. If, on the other hand, he cast his words as a fictitious apology, he would escape the suspicion of novelty and would rather win his hearers over by it, since all people are naturally inclined to give their goodwill to those who are getting the worst of it. That is why he blames accusers and slanderers and makes them the reason for his discourse. So that his craft may become evident to all, it will do no harm to hear the preface of his text. It runs as follows. (60) Two ancient manuscripts: katabalomenos; the editions: kataballomenos. [?] Read 'in impiety', as [?] the Latin.

EUNOMIUS. We know that slandering and maligning people with an unbridled tongue and an unfeeling mind is the work of wicked and quarrelsome men; but that those who have been thought wicked because of slander should try with all eagerness to turn the falsehood aside by refutation is the part of sensible men, who together with their own good counsel set great store by the safety of the many. BASIL. Such, then, is the form of his discourse, the kind one would expect from a man who does nothing simply or without guile. He overshadows the suspicion of innovation with the veil of an apology, and he hunts for goodwill from his hearers, as though slander had forced him to these words. But his staging of an apology is exposed. Since he has no accuser to name for the charge he pretends to be contesting, he slips into a faceless drama of defense. It is not out of forbearance that he refrains from naming those who have wronged him (how could that be, when he drenches his opponents in so many insults?). Rather, he sees how glaring the falsehood would be, and he is ashamed to fasten on himself any definite accusers. For if he had been able to name anyone, he would certainly have said so and shouted it aloud, if not to satisfy his own anger, then at least to provide for the safety of the many, for whom he professes the greatest concern. Hidden wickedness is more harmful than wickedness publicly proclaimed. So if we had known the slanderers, we would more easily have escaped their 'unbridled tongues' and 'unfeeling minds', to use the very words of this most wise man. But since at the time, for whatever reason, he kept silent, let him be asked now, let him answer now: Who are the accusers who forestalled him with slanders and so made an apology necessary for him? From what world did they come? Who are the judges before whom he conducts the contest? In what court did he enter this suit? Where on land or sea was it convened? What could they say? At Seleucia? But there they were convicted by their own silence: although those assembled repeatedly summoned them to account for the charges brought against them, they did not appear, and for this they were condemned at that time. For my argument is directed in common to the whole faction together, which (67) Two codices: 'let him answer' (apokrinestho); the editions: apokrinastho [?] Some manuscripts: 'entered the suit'. [?] broken away from the healthy body of the Church. Or was it in Constantinople? But there no apology or speeches were needed. They had made allies of the men of the imperial court and of the others with the greatest power, and so they handled affairs with an overwhelming advantage. They were accusers, judges, executioners, everything they wished to be, when they expelled some of the bishops, installed others, and held the threat of death over others still, while with great licence they divided the cities among themselves. One of them, driven out of a city in Syria, seized Constantinople as if for a tyranny. This invincible and formidable speechwriter himself carried off Cyzicus as the prize of his impiety. And to Theodosius, after he had been convicted of unspeakable blasphemies, the Church of Sardis was handed over. I say nothing of the Bithynians, the Paphlagonians, the Cilicians, and all those on whom the evil fed as it spread around. What occasion was there for an apology then? But I think that even if he wanted to, he could not lie about this. So it is truer than anything that the form of his discourse is a device for deception. So much for that. Now consider what he writes a little further on. For it is perhaps not useless, before refuting his impiety, to point out a little of his conceit. 3. EUN. I ask you above all, both those who will hear now and those who will read later, not to want to tell falsehood from truth by numbers, attaching the better to the larger party; [?] etc. Shortly after, some manuscripts: 'having power through themselves'. Then the editions: 'they themselves and'. But the particle 'and' [?] Second [?]: 'and Eudoxius, of [?], etc.' [Of Antioch]. He succeeded Macedonius, having been installed by Constantine in his place as bishop of Constantinople; on [ascending?] its throne he uttered that notorious saying: 'The Father is impious, the Son pious', the one as revering no one, the other as revering the Father. Two manuscripts: 'later'.

BAS. What are you saying? Are we not to give more weight to those who came before us? Are we not to respect the multitude of Christians now living, and of all who have lived since the Gospel was proclaimed? Are we not to take account of the standing of those who have shone in every kind of spiritual gift, to all of whom this wicked road of impiety that you have newly opened is hateful and hostile? Are we instead simply to close the eyes of our souls, banish from our minds the memory of every saint, and each bring his own heart, empty and swept clean, to lay it open to your deceptions and sophistries? You would indeed have seized great power if what the devil failed to obtain by all his various schemes you were able to obtain by command: if, persuaded by you, we were to judge the tradition that has prevailed through all past time among so many saints to be of less worth than your impious invention. But it is not enough for him to steal away the reasoning of those who hear him now; he demands that those who come upon his discourse at some later time should hold the same opinion. Oh, the arrogance! To think that his discourse will last for later generations, and that his memory will be preserved immortal for all time to come! And this is the boast of the man who, a little later, plays the coy one before his hearers, as if he cared nothing for conceit, speaking thus to the judges of his drama. EUN. Further, not to be angry with us if, disregarding conceit and fear, and preferring freedom from fear for the things to come over immediate favor and safety, and judging the threat appointed for the impious to be more fearsome than any earthly suffering or temporal death, we set forth, stripped of every covering, the

gentlemen, and who has climbed to the very summit of virtue, risen above earthly things, and transferred his whole way of life to heaven! This is a novel kind of arrogance. By the very words with which he pretends to disregard conceit, he lifts himself to the utmost pitch of self-inflation. For if the conduct for which he suggests he deserves to be pardoned consists of the chief points of the Gospel life, he leaves us to guess what sort of man he must think himself in the things he has achieved. These remarks, which convey as it were the character of his whole purpose, are enough, though much has been passed over in silence. By his lies we may recognize the father of lies speaking in him, and from his boasting learn with whom he is condemned, since the Apostle says plainly that whoever is puffed up falls into the condemnation of the devil. Let us now come to the refutation of his impiety itself. 4. First he sets out a creed made up of simple and undefined expressions. Some of the Fathers also used it, not to address questions under dispute, but simply speaking among themselves in simplicity of heart. Perhaps Arius too, as they say, put it forward to Alexander in order to deceive him (for this too is reported). Be that as it may, Eunomius puts it forward as agreeing with his own opinion, for two reasons. One is to escape the suspicion of innovation by accepting the creed of the Fathers as correct. The other is that everyone, trusting in the simplicity of these words, might fall unawares into the snares of his sophistries. At the same time he saw this too: that he would be able to slip in his own opinion plausibly while supposedly interpreting the words of the Fathers, and would most probably escape detection in his impiety; or, if he were caught, he would seem blameless, as one saying nothing of his own but merely acting as the interpreter of another's thought. In doing this he made a most ridiculous blunder without noticing it. For after praising the creed at great length and in lofty terms, a little further on he heaps the most shameful reproaches on it. But to make my meaning clearer, I will divide his discourse into parts and examine it. First let us learn what creed he puts forward, setting out his very words. EUN. 'The pious tradition,' he says, 'that has prevailed from of old from the Fathers, let us first set out as a kind of standard and rule, and use it as an exact criterion for judging what is said.'

BAS. Of the contradiction in what he said, and the shameless conflict of his statements with one another, we will speak a little later. But first let us remind ourselves that this is the man who earlier in his discourse very grandly promised us to set out the truth stripped of every covering. Here, then, it ought to have been written: 'We believe that unbegottenness is the essence of the God of the universe,' or, 'We believe that the Only-begotten is unlike the Father in essence.' He would have written this if, as he promised, he were not overshadowing his own opinion with a deceitful curtain. But, I think, since he uses all his words treacherously, he keeps his own views to himself, so as not to make himself unconvincing and hard to accept by striking untrained ears. Instead he puts forward the creed of the Fathers. Because its terms are neutral, it would offer no obstacle to the whole construction of his argument, and it would easily follow along when, under the guise of interpretation, he steered the discourse toward what he [wished?]. That this is true is evident at once. For as soon as he has set the creed out, he leaps straight into interpretation, [?] saying that it needs some other [?], and that it is not sufficient to clear him of the charge. Why then did you put it forward at all, instead of coming straight to those words that were both precise and would have freed you from the charges? As it is, he puts it forward as a safe criterion, and then corrects it again as though it had nothing sound in it. And this is plain to everyone: like a hook that drags its victim to death, he wraps around his own opinion Third Royal manuscript: 'and in the Holy Spirit'. the simplicity of the faith, like a kind of bait, so that the less experienced, rushing at what they see, may be caught unguarded on the evil of impiety. But he did not want to seem to be correcting, without any need, the creed he himself had exalted with extravagant praise. So consider how, as if forgetting his own words, he disparages it. EUN. This, then, is the simpler faith, common to all who care to seem or to be Christians, stated summarily, as in passing. BAS. Tell me: is the pious tradition of the Fathers, which you yourself called the rule, the standard, the safe criterion, now to be called an instrument of deceit, an art of pretense, and the like? For if it fits not those who are truly Christians but those who have valued seeming over being, what else can one suppose about it but this? Who, unless he were completely out of his mind, would say that the rule of what is straight fits those whose souls are crooked, and that the standard of truth fits the enemies of truth? Those who have valued being called Christians over truly being Christians, and who put on this pretense to deceive the many, are far from all straightness and truth. So neither will the crooked be made straight, as the word of Ecclesiastes says, nor will the criteria of truth fit those who have chosen falsehood as their way of life, as he supposes. 5. It was for the reasons I have mentioned that he was carried into such obvious contradictions: by praising the creed he hoped to seem to share the piety of the Fathers, and by finding fault with it again he hoped to open the way for his own interpretation. That is why he calls the same thing a rule and also says that it needs a more exact addition. Let this also serve as a sign of his utter ignorance, if anyone cares to examine this point too. A rule, most wise sir, and a standard, so long as they lack nothing of being a rule and a standard, admit no addition for the sake of exactness. An addition is made only where something is lacking. And if they are incomplete, they could no longer properly bear these names. So much for that. Now let us examine the statements he sets out about God. EUN. There is, then, he says, one God, confessed by us both according to our natural notion and according to the teaching of the Fathers, who came into being neither from himself nor from another. For each of these is equally impossible,

since in truth the maker must exist before what comes into being, and what is made must come second to its maker. Nor can a thing be prior or posterior to itself, nor can anything else exist before God. For in that case that other thing would have held the [?] of deity before the second

BASIL. Why, then, have I set out this whole passage of his? So that the idle chatter the man indulges in throughout his treatise may become plain. He himself says that it is evident to the common notions of everyone that God is unbegotten, and yet he undertakes to bring us proofs of it. He is doing much the same as someone who, at high noon, wanted to teach people with healthy eyesight by argument that the sun is the brightest of the stars in the sky. But if one who proves by argument what is known through the senses is ridiculous [?] … to learn that the unbegotten has not been begotten, either by himself or by another, and that he is neither older nor younger than himself? What, then, is he after with all this? It seems to me that he is, for one thing, preening himself on his chains of inference, as though he were shrewd and extraordinary in intellect, quick to suspect an absurdity and quicker still to resolve what he has detected. That is why he revels in the twists of his arguments and labours over the fine points of his proof that the unbegotten was begotten neither by himself nor by another. And yet not even here does he forget his own craft. While dwelling on what everyone agrees on, he slips in for himself certain elements, as it were, for the arguments that follow. For it is not idly that he includes the statement that in truth the maker must exist before what comes into being. But if one who proves by argument what is known through the senses is ridiculous, how can one who teaches what the common preconceptions already agree on not be guilty of the same folly? Surely, to sensible people, these things are far more credible than what appears to the eye. Now if there were someone who shamelessly opposed this truth and insisted that the unbegotten had been begotten, either from himself or from another, then the clumsiness of what he says might perhaps be excused. But to this day no one, either among those outside our faith or among those within the Church itself who have risen up against the truth, has reached such a pitch of madness as to dispute the unbegottenness of the unbegotten. So I fail to see what is gained by these arguments. Did we really need the syllogisms of Aristotle and Chrysippus to learn that the unbegotten has not been begotten, either by himself or by another, and that he is neither older nor younger than himself? even if it seems to agree with our notions, it is found nowhere in Scripture and is the first element of their blasphemy, so I would say it rightly deserves to be passed over in silence. After all, the word "Father" carries the same force as "unbegotten", and it also brings in with it, through the relation, the notion of the Son joined to it. For he who is truly and solely Father is from no one else, and "from no one" is the same as "unbegotten". So we ought not to call him Unbegotten rather than Father, unless we mean to be wiser than the teaching of the Saviour, who said, "Go and baptize in the name of the Father," and not "of the Unbegotten." So much for that. Let us now examine how his argument continues. Going on a little further, and summing up for himself, as it were, what he has said, he writes as follows. EUNOMIUS. If, then, it has been shown that neither he himself nor anything else exists before him, but that he is before all things, then unbegottenness follows upon him; or rather, he himself is unbegotten substance. BASIL. The trickery we have detected in these words is, I think, quite easy to see for anyone who pays even a little attention, but not easy to make plain to the many. Still, we must try, setting our hope on him who gives the word to those who preach the gospel with great power. He has said that if neither he himself nor anything else exists before him, unbegottenness follows upon him. Then he realized that the sequence of his premises had brought the argument round to the opposite of what he wanted. For if unbegottenness follows upon God, it plainly accompanies him from outside, and what is outside God is not his substance. That would make his clumsy contrivance dissolve and vanish. So, to avoid this, what does he do? Caring little for the ridicule he was bound to incur for saying things that do not follow, he steered the argument by means of a correction toward what he wanted, saying, "Or rather, he himself is unbegotten substance." But this does not agree in any way with what came before. For how can God have unbegottenness both as something that follows upon him (11) The editions read "in the name of the Father" … "of the Father, and not of the Unbegotten" … "let us examine." The old books [?] … "to exist before him has been shown" [?] … "Or rather, he himself is unbegotten substance" [?].

and also not as something that follows, but as something contained in the definition of his substance? Even so, he does not let his sophism be completely destroyed. For if, having said that unbegottenness follows upon him, he had stopped the argument there, he would have had no way either to call unbegottenness the substance of the God of all, or to show that the only-begotten Son is alien to him in substance itself. Nothing that follows from outside could sever the kinship of Father and Son in substance itself. But by adding "Or rather, he himself is unbegotten substance," he has indicated that what God is, is unbegottenness. How much this prepares the way for his impious undertaking I shall show a little further on in the argument. So, then, what he said at first emerged from the truth of things, following the sequence of his premises. But what he added at the end was flung in from his heretical mindset, as this most shameless of all speechwriters leapt to correct his statement. For how can the same thing both follow upon God and be identical with him, when it is obvious to everyone that what follows is something other than that of which it is a consequence? But he, as though he had found himself a road, sets out from the statement he had snatched in advance and proceeds to establish that unbegottenness is the substance of the God of all. Once this has been shown, he means to have it granted that the Only-begotten is unlike the Father in substance. But let us hear what he says. (21) (19) The editions read "being [alien] in substance." Three ancient books read "in substance itself."

unbegottenness in the case of God. He thinks that this will make it easy for him to argue that unbegottenness is the substance of God, and from there to show incontrovertibly that the only-begotten Son is unlike the Father in substance itself. That is why he attacks the word "conception", as though it meant nothing at all and existed in utterance alone. He also pretends that it is unworthy of God to honour him with conceptions. As for me, I do not yet insist on whether unbegottenness is contemplated by conception or not, until the examination of the argument itself has taught us. 6. But I would gladly ask him this very question: what is conception? Does this word signify nothing whatever, and is it merely a noise falling from the tongue? Such a thing would be called not conception but rather derangement and nonsense. But suppose he grants that conception does signify something, only something wholly false and unreal, like the centaurs and chimeras that myth-makers dream up. How, then, will the falsehood it signifies vanish along with the noise of the tongue, when the voice is poured out into the air while the false notions remain in the mind? The soul may fill itself with wholly false and empty fabrications, whether in images seen in sleep or in other idle motions of the mind, and keep them in memory, and then choose to announce them aloud. Even then the phantasms do not vanish together with the spoken word. Telling lies would be worth a great deal if the nature of a falsehood perished along with the words spoken; but that is not how it is by nature. It remains to show how common usage employs conception, and for what kinds of things, and how the divine oracles have taken up its use. We see, then, that in ordinary usage there are things which seem simple and single to the mind's overall grasp, but appear complex under detailed examination and are divided by the mind into many. These are said to be divisible by conception alone. (26) The Paris edition reads "that unbegottenness is the substance of God" [?] … "of false notions remaining"; from which codex the others [?]

For example, at first encounter a body seems simple, but reason, going over it, shows it to be complex. By conception it resolves the body into the things it is composed of: colour, shape, resistance, size, and the rest. Again, there are things with no real existence at all, which only a mental picture [?] and the imagination shape, such as everything that myth-makers and painters invent [?] to astonish those who come across them. These too are said in common usage to be contemplated by conception. This man mentions none of these, whether from ignorance or from malice, and has philosophized to us only about the conception of things that do not exist. And even that he does not explain as its nature is. For he does not say that conception signifies something, but something false; he says that the word is entirely meaningless and exists in utterance alone. Yet the word "conception" is so far from being used only for idle and unreal imaginings that, after the first notion arising in us from the senses, the subtler and more precise reflection on what has been thought is called conception. That is why common usage calls it "reasoning", though not in the proper sense. For example, everyone has a simple notion of grain, by which we recognize it when it appears. But when we examine it closely, we consider several more things and use different names to signify what we have thought. For we call the same grain now fruit, now seed, and again food: fruit, as the outcome of past farming; seed, as the beginning of future farming; and food, as fit to be added to the body of whoever eats it. Each of these is contemplated by conception, and none of them passes away with the noise of the tongue; rather, the notions are lodged in the soul of the one who thought them. In short, all things known through the senses, which seem to be one in their underlying subject but admit of a varied account when contemplated, are said to be contemplated by conception.

7. We have been taught by divine Scripture a use of conception close to this kind. I will pass over everything else, though I have much to say, and mention only the most pertinent case. Our Lord Jesus Christ, in what he says about himself, makes known to human beings the Godhead's love for humanity and the grace of the economy of salvation. He signified these by certain properties contemplated in him, calling himself the door, the way, the bread, the vine, the shepherd and the light, though he is not [?] (33) That whole phrase, "That is why common usage calls it reasoning" [?]

someone with many names, for not all of these names amount to the same thing. What "light" signifies is one thing, what "vine" signifies another, what "way" another, and what "shepherd" another. Yet being one in his underlying subject, one substance, simple and uncompounded, he names himself differently at different times, adopting titles that differ from one another by conception. For according to the difference of his activities and his relation to those who receive his benefits, he gives himself different names. He calls himself the light of the world, both to signify by this name the unapproachable glory of the Godhead and because he illuminates with the brightness of knowledge those who have purified the eye of the soul. He calls himself the vine, because he nourishes those rooted in him by faith so that they bear the fruit of good works. And he calls himself bread, because he is the most fitting food of a rational being: he holds the soul's constitution together and preserves its distinctive character, always supplying from himself what it lacks and not letting it sink into the weakness that comes from irrationality. Going through each of the names in this way, one would find various conceptions of one and the same subject, which in substance underlies them all. Who, then, has so sharpened his tongue for blasphemy as to dare to say that these conceptions dissolve together with the sounds? What is absurd, then, about taking certain things in the same way, by conception, in the case of the God of all, and first of all this very term that has set our whole discussion in motion? For we shall find that unbegottenness is spoken of in no other way. We say that the God of all is incorruptible and unbegotten, addressing him by these names according to different ways of approaching him. When we look back to the ages behind us and find that the life of God reaches beyond every beginning, we call him unbegotten. When we stretch our minds forward to the ages to come, we call him who is unbounded, infinite and comprehended by no end incorruptible. So just as the endlessness of his life is called incorruptible, its beginninglessness is called unbegotten, since we contemplate each by conception. What argument, then, will deny that each of these names is both conceived and an acknowledgment of what truly belongs to God? But he sets these apart from each other as conflicting and wholly incompatible: that something is said by conception, and that it fulfils for God the acknowledgment that he is what he is. "I am, and I have not changed," we learn the ever-sameness and immutability of the divine substance. How, then, is it not plain madness to say that no proper meaning underlies each of the names, but that, [?] the activity (53), all the names can be defined as identical with one another? But he might say that he has applied this scruple only to the title "unbegotten" and is unguarded about the others. Then let us ask him again: what is this arbitrary choice? 8. Nor let us pass over this point: what a show of piety he has devised to overthrow his hearers, when he says, EUNOMIUS. We should not honour God by human conception with the title "unbegotten", but pay him the most necessary debt of all, by acknowledging that he is what he is. BASIL. What words could do justice to the crookedness of these artifices? He tries to frighten the simpler folk, as though they were not rendering to God what is owed him unless they confess that unbegottenness is substance. He calls his own impiety the payment of a debt, so as not to seem to be saying anything of his own but to be fulfilling what is necessarily owed to God. And he shows the rest that if they place unbegottenness in the substance, they will be let off without account. But if they understand it otherwise, in the pious way, they will incur inexorable wrath for having failed to make the oldest and most necessary payment of all debts. I would gladly question him, then: does he observe this scruple equally with everything said of God, or only with this one word? If he contemplates nothing at all by conception, so as not to seem to honour God with human titles, he will have to confess that everything predicated of God is equally substance. How, then, is it not ridiculous to say that his creative power is substance, or again that his providence is substance, or likewise his foreknowledge, and in short to make every activity a substance? And if all these point to one meaning, the names must necessarily be equivalent to one another, as with things that have several names, as when we call the same man Simon and Peter and Cephas. Then whoever hears of God's unchangeableness will be led to his unbegottenness, and whoever hears of his being without parts will be carried off to his creative power. What could be more absurd than this confusion, which strips each name of its proper meaning and legislates against both common usage and the teaching of the Spirit? Yet when we hear that God made all things in wisdom, we are taught his creative skill. When we hear that he opens his hand and fills every living thing with his good pleasure, we learn of the providence that extends through all things. And when we hear that he made darkness his hiding place, we are taught the invisibility of his nature.

"I am, and I do not change": from this we learn that the divine essence is always the same and unchangeable. How then is it not plain madness to say that no proper meaning underlies each of the names, and that, against their natural force, all the names can be defined as meaning the same thing? Then, even if we grant this, they will gain nothing more for their purpose. For if all these terms, when applied to God the Father, signify his essence (I mean the unchangeable, the invisible, the incorruptible), then clearly they will likewise indicate essence when applied to the only-begotten Son of God. For we call the only-begotten Son too invisible, unchangeable, incorruptible, without parts, and everything of that kind. And so their cleverness will turn against them. They will not be able to prove him unlike in essence because of a difference in one appellation. Rather, because he shares in the many, the very necessity of their own premises will force them to confess him like. But suppose he says that he uses this scruple only with the word "unbegotten" and is not on his guard with the others. Then let us ask him again what this arbitrary choice is. So many things are said of God. Why show precision in this one alone, and why, while in this one he pays God the confession that he is what he is, does he not refuse in countless others to honour him with human conceptions? For a man who owes many debts is not so much honest in repaying one as he is grossly dishonest in withholding the many. So, like the craftiest of beasts, he is caught by his own tricks, and the very means by which he tries to escape notice expose him all the more. 9. Now consider what comes next in his argument. Having shown, as he thinks, that "unbegotten" cannot be understood by way of conception, he adds: EUNOMIUS: "But neither by way of privation, since privations are privations of what belongs to a thing by nature, and they come after the possessions." BASIL: It is not hard to show that he chatters this out of the wisdom of the world. That wisdom threw him headlong, and he took up these novel arguments. For the discussions of possession and privation belong to Aristotle, as those who have read him would say, in his work entitled the Categories, where he says that privations come after possessions. For our part, it would be enough to show that he speaks not from the teaching of the Spirit but from the wisdom of the rulers of this age, and then to say to him the words of the psalm: "The lawless have told me idle tales, but not as your law is, O Lord." Having learned that what he says does not come from the teachings of our Lord Jesus Christ, we could recall the Lord's own saying: "When he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own." In this way we could cut short much argument and make it plain to all at once that we have no fellowship with them. "For what agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what share has a believer with an unbeliever?" But so that we do not seem to take refuge in silence for lack of a refutation, come, let us discuss these points briefly too. We see, Eunomius, that many of the things said of God are expressed in the same form, such as "the incorruptible," "the immortal," "the invisible." We hold that "unbegotten" is of the same form. Now if some people call such terms privative, our argument is not with them. For we neither know the technical terminology of words nor envy those who know it. We will say only this: whatever class the other words we have listed are put in, the appellation "unbegotten" belongs to the same class. So, just as "incorruptible" signifies that corruption does not belong to God, and "invisible" that he transcends [Gloss: "unbegotten," Latin ingenitum.]

all apprehension through the eyes, and "incorporeal" that his essence is not extended in three dimensions, and "immortal" that dissolution will never befall him, so we say that "unbegotten" too shows that begetting does not belong to him. So if none of these names is privative, neither is that one. But if you grant that the others are said by way of privation and do not allow it for the appellation "unbegotten," tell me: what possession, coming first, does "incorruptible" show the privation of? And how can "unbegotten" not mean the same? But he plays tricks with this one word alone, because the starting points of his impiety hang on it. To make his trick plain, do this. Take the arguments he exercises on "unbegotten": that it cannot reasonably be said of God either by human conception or by privation. Transfer them to something else that is said of God, and examine them. You will find that they fit each case exactly. If you like, let us apply them to "incorruptible," carrying over his very wording: "In calling him incorruptible, we do not think we must honour him by human conception. We pay him the most necessary of all debts, the confession that he is what he is. But neither by way of privation, since privations are privations of what belongs to a thing by nature, and they come after the possessions." Why is it more fitting to philosophize like this about "unbegotten" than about "incorruptible," or indeed about every word expressed in the same form? But none of the others helps his impiety. That is why he does not even mention the rest, though the things said of God are countless. 10. The truth is this. No single name is enough to take in the whole nature of God and declare it adequately. Instead, many different names, each with its own meaning, gather together a notion of him. Compared with the whole, that notion is utterly faint and very slight, but it is enough for us. Among the names said of God, then, some indicate what belongs to God, and others the opposite, what does not belong to him. For from these two a kind of impression of God forms in us: from the denial of what is incongruous and from the confession of what is actually there. For example, when we call him incorruptible, we are in effect saying to ourselves or to our hearers, "Do not think that God is subject to corruption." When we call him invisible, we mean, "Do not suppose that he is grasped by the sense of sight" [Notes: "begetting to him" [?]. The editions read "could [mean] the"; but four manuscripts read "can." The editions read "by way of the privation"; the manuscripts lack the article. [?] concerning the words incorruptible, immortal, invisible.]

and when we call him immortal, "Never think that death befalls God." So too when we call him unbegotten, we mean, "Do not think that God's being depends on any cause or beginning." In short, each of these teaches us not to fall into unfitting notions in our conceptions of God. So, in order to recognize the distinctive property of God, we warn one another, when we speak about God, not to let our thoughts sink to what they should not, so that people may never think that God is one of the corruptible things, or the visible things, or the begotten things. All these prohibitive names are therefore a kind of renunciation of what is foreign to him: our mind is given clear shape and lays aside its notions of what does not belong to him. Again, we call God good, and just, and creator, and judge, and other such things. In the first case the words signified a kind of rejection and forbidding of what is foreign to God. Here, in the same way, they signify the positing and presence of what is proper to God and fittingly contemplated in him. So from each kind of appellation we are taught either that what belongs to him does belong, or that what does not belong does not. Now "unbegotten" signifies something that does not belong to him, for it shows that begetting does not belong to God. Whether one chooses to call this ablative, or prohibitive, or negative, or something of the sort, we will not quarrel. I think what has been said shows well enough that "unbegotten" does not signify something present in God. But the essence is not one of the things that do not belong to him. It is God's very being, and to count it among the things that are not is the height of insanity. For if the essence were among the things that are not, nothing else that is said of him could easily be anything at all. But it has been shown that "unbegotten" is ranked with what does not belong to him. So whoever holds that this word indicates the essence itself is wrong. 11. But he objects to anything being said of God by way of privation, as if that were absurd. So he takes refuge in what is supposedly more pious, placing "unbegotten" in the essence itself [Notes: (71) The editions read "placed among the things that do not belong." [?] seemed to himself to read "more impious"; [?] "takes refuge, and posits the unbegotten as the essence itself."]

and he brings his argument to its conclusion, writing as follows: EUNOMIUS: "Therefore, if it is neither by conception, nor by privation, nor in a part (for he has no parts), nor in him as something other than he (for he is simple), nor something other beside him (for he is one and alone unbegotten), he himself would be unbegotten essence."

BASIL: He has brought the argument where he wanted it. Having dragged "unbegotten" away from every other place, he has driven it, as he thought, into the essence itself, saying of the God of the universe that he himself would be unbegotten essence. I too would say that the essence of God is unbegotten. I would not say that unbegottenness is the essence. Next, this is worth noticing. "Without parts" and "simple" mean the same thing: what is without parts is what is not composed of parts, and what is simple, likewise, is what is not made up of many things. Yet he separates them as if they differed in their subject. Then he forbids us to divide God up, or to suspect that part of him is unbegotten and part begotten, or again to think that unbegottenness lies in him as one thing inside another. I shrink from refuting the emptiness of all this, for whoever argues against an idle talker seems somehow to become like him. That, I think, is why the wise Solomon advises us not to answer a fool according to his folly. For he has set out in his division arguments that no one ever stated or uttered, so that out of the many options he lists he may seem to find only one in which "unbegotten" is properly said. Perhaps we would need a longer argument to expose the falsehood and show that unbegottenness is not God's essence, if the items he listed in his division had not already been clearly refuted. But even if his argument had firmly established that "unbegotten" is understood neither by conception nor by privation, his conclusion would still not follow at all. For what necessity is there that unbegottenness should fall under one of the items he listed? All the same, he adds, as if it were necessarily bound up with his premises: "Therefore, if it is neither by conception, nor by privation, nor in any other of the ways listed, he himself would be unbegotten essence." So let us turn it around and say: "Therefore, since it is contemplated by conception and the name is privative, unbegottenness is not the essence of God." For as long as he does not [Note: "takes refuge, placing the unbegotten in the essence itself." They supply "in," so as to read "in placing ... in the essence."]

refute what has been said or give strength to his own premises, his conclusion will have no ground to stand on. 12. In general, to think that one has discovered the very essence of the God who is over all: what arrogance and conceit that is! For their boasting almost outshines even the one who said, "I will set my throne above the stars." These men do not lay bold claim to the stars or to heaven. They boast of entering into the very essence of the God of the universe. Let us question him: where does he say his comprehension of it came from? From the common notion? But that tells us that God is, not what he is. From the teaching of the Spirit, then? Which teaching? Where is it found? God revealed the hidden and secret things of his wisdom to the great David, and does David not openly confess that knowledge of God is out of reach, when he says, "Your knowledge is too wonderful for me; it is too strong, and I cannot attain to it"? And Isaiah, who was granted the vision of God's glory: what did he reveal to us about the divine essence? In his prophecy about Christ he solemnly declares, "Who will tell of his generation?" And Paul, the chosen vessel, who had Christ speaking in him, who was caught up to the third heaven, who heard unspeakable words that no human being may utter: what teaching about God's essence did he leave us? When he looked into the partial reasons of the divine economy, he grew dizzy, as it were, at a contemplation that no one can pass through to its end, and cried out, "O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!" If these things are out of reach even for those who have attained the measure of Paul's knowledge, how great is the conceit of those who claim to know the essence of God? I would gladly ask them about the earth they stand on and were made from. What do they say about it? What do they tell us its essence is? If they can discuss with us beyond dispute the things on the ground under our feet, then we may believe them when they hold forth on things beyond all thought. So what is the essence of the earth? How is it comprehended? Let them answer us: did reason reach it, or sense perception? If they say sense perception, by which of the senses can it be grasped? Sight? But sight perceives colours. Touch? But touch distinguishes hardness and softness, hot and cold, and the like, and no one would call any of these essence unless he had been carried off to the last extreme of insanity. As for taste and smell, what need is there [Notes: (78) The Colbert manuscript [?] reads "from the common essence"; perhaps from the third [?]: "God revealed openly, confess[es] [?]." [?] "But touch? This too."]

to speak of them? The one perceives flavours, the other vapours. Hearing perceives noises and voices, which have nothing to do with the earth. So all they have left is to claim that they found its essence by reason. What reason is that? Where in Scripture is it found? Which of the saints handed it down? 13. The one who told us about the creation taught us only this much: "In the beginning God made the heaven and the earth. And the earth was invisible and unformed." He thought it enough to proclaim the one who made it and set it in order. To busy himself with what its essence is he declined, as something vain and useless to his hearers. So if knowledge of it is confirmed neither by the testimony of the senses nor by the teaching of reason, where will they still say their comprehension of it came from? Whatever of it the senses perceive is colour, or bulk, or weight, or lightness, or density, or porousness, or resistance, or softness, or coldness, or heat, or the qualities of flavour, or the differences of shape. These men would not call any of these essence, however glibly they say everything else. Again, the earth has not been contemplated by reason by any of the wise and blessed men. What way of knowing it is still left? Let them answer us, these men who despise everything at their feet, pass beyond heaven and all the powers above the world, and join themselves by the mind to the first essence itself. But conceit seems to be the most grievous of all human passions, and truly to throw those in whom it arises into the devil's condemnation. That is why these men, who do not even know the nature of the earth they trample on, boast of entering into the very essence of the God of the universe. Consider God's saints, Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. Because they attained every virtue, God honoured them even with being named as their God, as something exceptional and fitting to his own majesty, and he called himself the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob: "For this is my eternal name," he says, "and my memorial to all generations." Yet to these men God did not even reveal his name, much less disclose what his essence is. "For I am the Lord," he says, "and I appeared to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, being their God, and my name I did not reveal to them": clearly because it was too great for human hearing to take in. But to Eunomius, it seems, [References: Genesis 1:1–2; Exodus 3:15; Exodus 6:2–3. Notes: (82) The editions read "differences, or size"; but "or size" [?]. [?] "let them answer us, those who despise all [?]." (84) The fourth Royal manuscript reads "of all human passions."]

God has shown not only his name but his very essence. This great secret, which was revealed to none of the saints, he himself publishes in whole books and blurts out thoughtlessly to everyone. The things laid up for us in the promises are beyond all human knowledge, and the peace of God surpasses all understanding. Yet he will not accept that the very essence of God is beyond all understanding and all human knowledge. 14. In my view, comprehending it is beyond not only human beings but every rational nature. By rational nature I mean here the one within creation. For the Father is known only to the Son and to the Holy Spirit: "No one knows the Father except the Son"; and "The Spirit searches all things, even the depths of God." "For no one knows," it says, "the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him; so too no one has known the things of God except the Spirit who is from God." What special knowledge, then, will they leave to the Only-begotten and the Holy Spirit, if they themselves comprehend the very essence? Surely, after assigning to the Only-begotten the contemplation of God's power, goodness and wisdom, they will not claim that understanding of the essence is within their own measure. Quite the contrary. It is likely that the essence itself is beyond the sight of all except the Only-begotten and the Holy Spirit, and that we are led upward from God's activities, conceive of the maker through the things he has made, and so gain an understanding of his goodness and wisdom. For this is "what can be known of God," which God has made plain to all people. Whatever the theologians seem to have written about God's essence in figures of speech or allegories, those words point to other meanings. So if anyone insists, without examination, on standing by the bare letter in its obvious sense, he will turn aside to Jewish myths and old wives' tales and grow old utterly poor in worthy thoughts about God. For besides conceiving God's essence as something material, and so agreeing with the godless among the Greeks, he will also suppose it to be varied and composite. The prophet relates that God is of amber from the loins upward and that his lower parts are made of fire. Whoever does not rise to higher thoughts [Notes: [?] "his own [essence] ..."; then the editions read "and so great the secret" [?] "secret" lacks the article. (91) Not a few manuscripts read "the spirit, the one in him" [?]; [?] "except spirit, the" [?]. We chose [to follow] the old [?] "the" [?].]

will be taught the essence of God by Ezekiel, then hear from Moses that God is fire, and be carried off by the wise Daniel to yet other notions. So he will be found gathering from the Scriptures imaginings that are not only false but in conflict with one another. Let us give up, then, our curiosity about the essence, since it cannot be reached, and obey the simple exhortation of the Apostle, who says: "For one must first believe that God exists and that he rewards those who seek him." It is not searching out what he is, but confessing that he is, that prepares salvation for us. Since, then, it has been shown that the essence of God is beyond the grasp of human nature and wholly beyond words, it remains to discuss his unbegottenness: what it is, and how it is contemplated in the God of the universe.

15. When we reason it out, then, we find that the notion of "unbegotten" comes to us not from inquiring what he is, but rather (if I may force the expression) from inquiring how he is. For our mind asks whether the God who is over all has some cause above himself. Then, unable to conceive of any, it calls the beginninglessness of his life "unbegotten." When we speak about human beings and say, "So-and-so was born of so-and-so," we are not describing what each of them is, but where he came from. In the same way, when we speak of God, the word "unbegotten" signifies not what he is, but that he comes from nowhere. What I mean may become clearer this way. Luke the evangelist sets out the genealogy according to the flesh of our God and Saviour Jesus Christ, going back from the last to the first. He began with Joseph and said that he was the son of Heli, and Heli the son of Matthat, and so, tracing back step by step, he brought his account up to Adam. Then, coming to the earliest, he said that Seth was of Adam and Adam was of God, and there he ended his ascent. In telling of each one's birth he was not showing the essences of those he listed. He was setting out the immediate origin from which each one came. So, just as he said that

Adam is from God. So let us ask ourselves: and God, from what? Is it not ready to hand in everyone's mind that he is from nothing? And "from nothing" is plainly the unoriginate, and the unoriginate is the unbegotten. So just as in the case of human beings "being from someone" was not the substance, so too in the case of the God of all it is not possible to say that "unbegotten" is the substance, since it amounts to the same thing as "from nothing." Whoever says that the unoriginate is the substance acts much as someone would who, asked what Adam's substance is and what his nature is, answered that he was not formed from the union of man and woman but by the divine hand. "But I am not asking about the manner of his coming into existence," one might say, "but about the material substrate of the man himself, which I am far from learning from your answer." The same happens to us too: from the word "unbegotten" we are taught the "how" of God rather than his very nature. 16. In general, if anyone wishes to learn the truth of what we are saying, let him examine himself whenever he wishes to think something about God, and see whether he arrives at the meaning of "unbegotten." For I see this. When we stretch our mind toward the ages to come, we call "endless" the one whose life is bounded by no limit. In the same way, when we climb in our reasonings to what lies above the ages, and peer as if into some vast sea, into the boundlessness of God's life, we cannot lay hold of any beginning from which it came to be. Instead we conceive God's life as always beyond and overflowing whatever we can conceive, and we have called this beginninglessness of life "unbegotten." For this is the meaning of "the unbegotten [?]": not having the beginning of one's being from somewhere else. But because the unbegotten is contemplated in the God of all alone, he has most villainously of all seized on it to blaspheme the Only-begotten. For what does he say as he goes on? EUNOMIUS: Being unbegotten, according to the preceding demonstration, he would never admit generation so as to share his own nature with the one begotten, and he would escape all comparison and communion with the begotten. BASIL: O the shameless

[?] to the God and Father, in order to show the Only-begotten Son and God [?], he keeps silent about the names of Father and Son and speaks simply of unbegotten and begotten. He hides the names of the saving faith and hands on the bare doctrines of blasphemy. That way, once the impiety has been laid bare in the realities and then carried over to the persons, he himself may seem to have said nothing blasphemous, yet he has the blasphemy built up by the sequence of his argument. "Being unbegotten," he says, "he would escape all comparison and communion with the begotten." He did not say "Father and Son," but "unbegotten and begotten." That is one piece of villainy of this sort; now consider what the other is. He may rely on the words of blessed Peter recorded in the Acts of the Apostles, where he says, “Let all the house of Israel know that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified.” But first, the testimony has nothing to do with the question. He promised to show that the saints called the Son a thing made, and then offers a testimony about God the Father, saying that he made. Surely he would not claim to be free, in discussing matters of such weight, to invent derivations and reshapings of words. How then is it safe to remodel the word “made” and call the maker of all things a thing made? If such a title suited him, the Spirit would not have kept silent about it.
