Yet what sensible person would agree with this argument, that things with different names must also differ in substance? Peter and Paul, and in short all human beings, have different names, but all have one substance. That is why we are the same as one another in most respects, and differ from one another only by the distinctive properties seen in each. So names signify not substances but the particular features that mark out each individual. When we hear “Peter,” then, we do not understand his substance from the name (by substance I here mean the material substrate, which the name does not signify at all), but we form a notion of the properties seen in him. For from this word we at once think of the son of Jonah, the man from Bethsaida, the brother

of Andrew, the one called from among fishermen to the ministry of apostleship, the one who because of his surpassing faith received upon himself the building of the Church. None of these is the substance, understood as the subsistence [?]. So the name marks out for us the character of Peter, but nowhere presents the substance itself. Again, when we hear “Paul,” we think of a combination of other properties: the man of Tarsus, the Hebrew, as to the law a Pharisee, the disciple of Gamaliel, the zealous persecutor of the churches of God, the one brought to knowledge by the terrifying vision, the apostle of the Gentiles. All these are summed up by the one word “Paul.” And yet, if it were true that things whose names differ have contrary substances, then Paul and Peter, and in short all human beings, would have to be of different substances from one another. But no one is so ignorant, so blind to our common nature, as to be led to say this. “For you were formed from clay,” it says, “just as I was.” These words signify nothing other than that all human beings are of one substance. So he who argues sophistically that difference of substance follows from difference of names is wrong. The nature of things does not follow their names; rather, names were found after the things. For if this were true, then things that share the same names would also have to have one and the same substance. And since those perfect in virtue have been thought worthy of the name “God,” human beings would be consubstantial with the God of the universe. But just as saying this is plain madness, so that other argument is gripped by the same insanity. [Apparatus:] Basil: “substance understood… the subsistence” [?]. The editions read “marks out the… of Peter” [?]; we [?] “the person of Peter.”

…calling the Only-begotten a thing made, our ears would not already have been deafened by its being dinned into them. Then he says that because of those who suppose the Lord's generation to be bodily, and who stumble over words with more than one meaning, he must speak briefly about these things too. Yet what stopped him from first confirming his own argument with testimonies from Scripture, and only then going on to correct the weaker brethren and to remedy the harm caused by ambiguous words, if such harm has ever come to anyone or ever will? For who is so wholly fleshly in mind, and so unversed in the divine words, that on hearing of a divine generation he sinks to bodily imaginings: the union of male and female, conception in the womb, formation and shaping, and emergence into the world at the due time? Who is so like a beast that on hearing that God the Word came forth from God, and that Wisdom was begotten from God, he falls in his thoughts to the passions of the body? 6. But along with everything else, he has devised this too as a respectable cover for his words: he wants to seem to take on the labor of teaching out of compassion for the less intelligent brethren. He supposedly corrects the bodily notions that arise from this title, yet does nothing to avert the harm done by calling the Lord a thing made. Yet the one who imagines the generation to be bodily would also be carried down to material ways of making. Surely the weak person will not conceive, from the word “beget,” some division, transfer and outflow of the begetter's substance, and yet not be led to suppose matter brought in from outside, out of non-being, to make up the subsistence of the thing made, as you put it. Why then does he heal only half of his brethren's infirmities of thought? Why does he care for those who suppose a bodily generation, but overlook those who stumble over the title “thing made”? Because he knows that “begotten” is hostile to his doctrines, since the one begotten must surely be akin to the begetter and identical in nature with him, whereas “made” is friendly to his premises and fights on their side, because of the alien
and foreign, and to present a notion wholly alien to the one who made it. Then he adds to this:

EUNOMIUS: We therefore call the Son an offspring, according to the teaching of the Scriptures. We do not take the essence to be one thing and what is signified to be something else beside it. Rather, it is the very hypostasis which the name signifies, since the designation is truly applied to the essence.

BASIL: Here too, then, he openly fights against the truth, yet he speaks consistently with himself. In the earlier arguments he defined "unbegotten" as signifying the essence of the God of the universe. In the same way he says here that "offspring" signifies the essence of the Son, so that through the antithesis of begotten and unbegotten he may show the Only-begotten to be opposite to the Father in his very essence. For this reason he lays down words that lie outside the usage of the divine Spirit, and names the Son "offspring." Where did he get this? From what teaching? Which prophet, which of the apostles, gave him this designation? I have found this word used in this way nowhere in Scripture. 7. And yet he boasts that he has taken these designations from nowhere but the teaching of the Spirit. It is a small thing to him to make war on human beings unless he also ventures against the Spirit himself. That the Father has begotten we have been taught in many places; but that the Son is an "offspring" we have not heard to this very day. "For a child has been born to us," it says, "a son has also been given to us; and his name is called" not "offspring" but "Angel of Great Counsel." Yet if "offspring" signified essence, the Spirit would have taught us no other name than the one that was going to present his essence plainly. And again, Peter, who was counted worthy of those blessings for his knowledge of the truth, did not say, "You are the offspring," but "You are the Christ, the Son of the living God." And Paul, who filled all his writing with the designation "Son," will be seen nowhere to have mentioned "offspring." Yet this man puts the word forward with great confidence, as though he had received it from the divine school. For not even here should we concede to him the [?] (Note 55: the Colbert codex reads "signifies the essence of God" [?]. Note 40: Codex [?] reads "For not even that which.")

[?] One who has been trained in the fear of God ought rather to be content with this: to abide by the names found in Scripture and through them to render the doxology in a manner worthy of God. Those who first translated the Hebrew language into Greek did not venture to translate certain names, but carried over the Hebrew word itself, such as Sabaoth, Adonai, Eloi and the like. They showed this reverence not only with the divine names but with many others as well. If they did so, how much fear ought we to have regarding the names of the Lord? When would they have brought themselves to invent names of their own, when they did not even dare to translate some, lest the vividness of the meaning be weakened by an ill-fitting rendering? 8. "But if God begot," he says, "why should we not call the one begotten an offspring?" Because it is a fearful thing for us to address him with names of our own, God has granted him the name that is above every name. "You are my Son," he says, "today I have begotten you." By their reasoning it would have been more consistent for him to be called "offspring" rather than "Son," because he was begotten; but that was not said. Therefore whoever keeps the judgment seat of Christ before his eyes, and knows how great the danger is of taking anything away from what the Spirit has handed down or adding anything to it, must not be eager to innovate on his own account. He must rest content with what the saints proclaimed before him. To venture, then, upon a word that neither common usage nor the usage of the Scriptures has accepted: how is that not the height of folly? What father or mother, kindly and gently disposed toward their own child, would stop calling him son or child and address him as "offspring"? Scripture says, "Child, go into the vineyard"; and elsewhere, "God will provide himself a sheep for the slaughter, my child"; and again Isaac asks, "Who are you, my child?"; and "Son, do not make light of the Lord's discipline"; and "A wise son gladdens his father"; and so on. Nowhere is anyone shown addressing his own child as "offspring." The reason is clear. "Son" and "child" are names of living beings, but "offspring" is not always so. Even what is expelled in a miscarriage before it has taken shape can be called an offspring, yet such a thing does not merit the name "child." The fruits of the earth are called "produce" (literally "offspring"), but they are not called children: "I will not drink," he says, "of this produce of the vine." We have rarely found this designation applied to living beings, and where it (Note: some printed books read "the judgment seat of Christ" [?]; but the manuscripts read "that of Christ." Note 46: the Colbert codex and a third [?] read "we have found this designation transferred to a living being.")

is so used, one can see that it is predicated of an animal and taken as an image of [?]. "Serpents," he says, "brood of vipers." For this reason, I think, common usage has held this designation in low esteem, and the divine Scripture plainly declines it, especially in speaking of the only-begotten Son of God. It did not even accept the designation "child," since that is heavily human. The Apostle makes this clear: again and again he calls the Lord "Son" and praises him with various other designations, "firstborn," "image" and "radiance," but he avoids the designation "offspring." If this man, or anyone else among the champions of his doctrine, can show it, we shall let them erase everything. But he could not, unless perhaps he imitates the impious Marcion, removing some of the divine oracles and inserting others. So foreign, then, is the word "offspring" to both common usage and the usage of the Scriptures. 9. Let us next see whether this name can be assigned to the very essence of the Son. For he says:

EUNOMIUS: It is impossible for the essence to be one thing and what is signified something else beside it. Rather, it is the very hypostasis which the name signifies, since the designation is truly applied to the essence.

BASIL: These doctrines of yours are truly worthy of the judges you have invented. You lay down laws with great license, as though in a marketplace of madmen or an assembly of drunkards, where no one either hears or understands what is said, and you think it enough, in place of any proof, that you yourself have said it. Does he not know that some names, uttered absolutely and by themselves, signify the things that underlie them, while others, said in relation to something else, indicate only their relation to that to which they refer? For instance, "man," "horse" and "ox" each present the very thing named. But "son," "slave" or "friend" indicate only the connection with the name joined to them. So whoever hears "offspring" is not carried in thought to some essence. He understands that it is connected with something else, for an offspring is called the offspring of someone. A word, then, that produces no conception of any substance,

but signifies only a relation to another: to lay down that this is essence, how is that not the height of derangement? Yet we showed a little earlier that even absolute names, however much they seem to indicate some subject, do not present the essence itself. They mark off certain properties concerning it. 10. But this most wise man, who has spent his whole life on vain arts, does not blush to say that "offspring" signifies the very essence of the Only-begotten. Consider how absurd this is. If the essence is offspring, and conversely whatever is offspring is essence, then all offspring will be of the same essence as one another. And what follows from this by his reasoning? The Creator of the universe will turn out to have the same essence as everything that has had a share in generation. He will surely not say that "offspring" signifies essence in the case of the Son, but no longer keeps the same sense in the case of the other things that partake of generation. If he does, let him state some clear and incontestable reason why the same designation does not carry equal force in every case alike. But he could not. Whatever definition of "offspring" he may devise will fit all begotten things alike. The greatest proof that this argument is true is the mind of each hearer. When he hears "So-and-so is the offspring of so-and-so," let each ask himself what notion is impressed on him. Is it that the one begotten is the essence of the one who begot him? Or is that laughable, and the truth rather that he was brought into being from him by way of generation? This, then, can fittingly be said of the Only-begotten and of any begotten being whatever. And since the relation is common to all, let no one think that this lowers the dignity of the Only-begotten. The Son does not differ from other things in standing in some relation. The supremacy of God over mortal things is revealed in the distinctive character of his essence. But consider into what absurdity their reasoning leads. An offspring is called the offspring of another, as common usage confirms and no one will deny. If in the case of the Son this very word signifies essence, as they reason, then it will be the essence of the one whose offspring it is called. By this sequence, then, the designation "offspring" will no longer signify the essence of the Only-begotten, as they insist, but that of the God of the universe. For if it is impossible to conceive the essence as one thing and the offspring as something else beside it, (Note: [?] reads "the hypostasis"; but in the margin [?]. Note 59: [?] "when he hears"; the manuscripts read "when he hears" [?]. Note 61: some codices read "both of the"; the printed editions read "of the.")

and to say "essence" and to say "offspring" mean the same thing, and the Son is the offspring of God, then he will be the essence of God, if "offspring" denotes the essence. And so, by his reasoning, the offspring will turn out to be the essence of the Unbegotten. If the conclusion is ridiculous, let the one who laid down the premises inherit the shame. It seems that once an argument has strayed from the truth, the logic of its error carries it into many dangerous absurdities. 11. These, then, are like preliminary bouts and preparations for the blasphemy. He brings out the chief point of the evil in what follows, saying:

EUNOMIUS: The essence of the Son was begotten, not existing before its own constitution, but it exists, having been begotten before all things by the will of the Father.

BASIL: He still clings to the same tricks. He discourses to us about the essence of the Son as though he meant the Son to be something other than it, and in this way he tames our ears in advance for the blasphemy. He does not say openly that the Son was begotten from things that are not, but that his essence was begotten when it did not exist. Did not exist before what? Tell me. Observe his sophistry. He compares the essence with itself, so that everyone will think he is saying something tolerable. He does not say that it did not exist before the ages, or simply that it did not exist, but that it did not exist before its own constitution. Tell me, do you say that the essence of the Father is older than its own constitution? If he does not subject the essence of the Son to time, and does not take the "before" in this statement in a temporal sense, then his argument is vain and idle and therefore not even worth answering. Yet anyone who wishes could transfer the same nonsense to the God of the universe just as well. To say that God did not exist before his own constitution and to say that he existed before himself are the same folly. But if he takes the "before" in a temporal sense regarding the essence of the Son, he will also say that his essence

was begotten from things that are not, or rather that the Son himself was, since it makes no difference to the meaning whether one puts it this way or that. First, he ranks the maker of the ages second to time, or to the ages if you like. Then, following his own blasphemies, he will say that the Father too was not Father from the beginning but became Father later. 12. Yet if it is good and fitting to the blessedness of God to be Father, how was what befits him not present from the beginning? They will surely attribute the lack either to ignorance of the better or to inability: to ignorance if he discovered the better later, to inability if he knew and understood it but failed to attain the best. But if (and it is not right to say this) it is not good for him to be Father, why did he change and choose the worse? Let the blasphemy recoil on those responsible for it. The God of the universe has been Father from infinity and never began to be Father. He was not prevented by any lack of power from fulfilling his will. Nor did he wait for some cycle of ages so that, as with human beings and the other animals, he might reach full age, acquire the power to beget, and then obtain what he desired; it is for madmen even to think and say such things. Rather, he has a fatherhood (if I may call it that) which extends as far as his own eternity. Therefore the Son too, being before the age and being always, never began to be. As long as there is a Father, there is also a Son, and the conception of the Son enters at once together with the conception of the Father. For the Father is evidently the Father of a Son. There is no beginning of the Father; the beginning of the Son is the Father; and between them there is nothing. How then did he not exist from the beginning (for this is what they mean in their sophisms by "before his own constitution")? He has nothing that can be conceived as prior to himself except the one from whom he has his being, who surpasses him not by an interval but is ranked before him as cause. The Son's communion with God the Father has therefore been shown to be eternal. Our mind passes from the Son to the Father through no void, and joins the Son to the Father without interval. What opening, then, is still left for the wicked blasphemy of those who say that he was brought into being from what is not, when nothing stands between them to divide them? 13. Moreover, their folly deserves (Note: but the manuscripts read "or thus." Note 68: the printed editions read "second to the ages"; but [?])

to be marveled at. They do not understand that when they say the Son is from things that are not, they make him younger not only than the Father, but also than whatever it is by which they separate the Only-begotten from the Father. If there were anything between Father and Son, it would necessarily be older than the Son's existence. What then would this be? What else but an age or a time? Whoever conceives of the Father's life as exceeding that of the Only-begotten must be measuring it by something. By what else would he say he found the excess, if not by an interval of ages or times? If this is true, then the Scripture is false that says the ages came to be through him, and that teaches that all things came to be through him, for the ages are obviously included in "all things." But if they say that they do not deny that the Son was begotten before the ages, let them not overlook what in their argument

14. Now that he has taken away the glory due to the Only-begotten, consider with what words he honors him.

EUNOMIUS: The essence of the Son, he says, exists, having been begotten before all things by the will of God the Father.

BASIL: He grants this to the Son as something great: that he is older than creation and exists before his own works. He reckons it enough for the glory of the Creator of the universe that he is ranked ahead of his own creatures. Having estranged him, as far as lies in his power, from communion with God the Father, he credits him with glory for being honored above creatures. Then, pushing the blasphemy to the point of shamelessness, he hems us in, as he thinks, with inescapable logical necessities.

EUNOMIUS: Either God begot the Son when he existed, he says, or when he did not exist. If he did not exist, let no one accuse me of audacity. But if he existed, the claim is not only absurd and blasphemous but the height of silliness, for what exists has no need of generation.

BASIL: This is the much-repeated sophism, devised long ago by others, but now perfected by these men with their brazen and shameless tongues. Let us first remind the hearers who this man is. He claims that the ignorance of the many, who understand the Son's generation in a human way, has forced him to use these arguments. He claims to lead untrained souls up from bodily conceptions to spiritual contemplation. Yet because animals that are born did not exist before they were born, and one born today did not exist yesterday, he transfers this very notion to the hypostasis of the Only-begotten. "Since he was begotten," he says, "he did not exist before his generation." So magnificently does he expound to us the generation of the Only-begotten, and with such arguments he sets right the infirmities of our brothers. If anyone deserves to hear the proverb "Physician, heal yourself," he does. What remedy shall we offer him for this strange disease of reasoning, other than the words the Holy Spirit spoke to us through the blessed John: "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God"? With these two expressions the evangelist shut off one [?] (Luke 4:23. John 1:1. [?])

[?] and another [?]. For one cannot conceive of anything older than the beginning, since it would no longer be a beginning if it had anything beyond itself. Nor is it possible to pass through the "was" in thought and peer out to the "when he was not." The notion that he was not cancels the "was." If "beginning" were one of the terms said in relation to something else, as in "the beginning of wisdom," "the beginning of a good way" and "In the beginning God made," then perhaps, since he subsists from such a beginning, one could pass beyond his generation in thought. But this sense of "beginning" is absolute and stands in no relation, and it indicates the supreme nature. How, then, is he not ridiculous who conceives of something beyond it, or tries to get past it by reasoning? The "was" also extends as far as this beginning, beyond which nothing lies. For the "was" here does not indicate existence in time, as in "There was a man in the land of Uz," "There was a man from Ramathaim" and "The earth was invisible." The evangelist himself showed us elsewhere what such a "was" means, when he said, "He who is, and who was, and the Almighty." As "is" is, so is "was": equally eternal and timeless. To say that he who was in the beginning did not exist neither preserves the notion of beginning nor joins the existence of the Only-begotten to it. What is older than the beginning is inconceivable, and the being of God's Word is inseparable from it. So however far you wish to run back in your mind's busy inquiries, you will not be able to pass beyond the "was" or get outside it in your reasonings.

I will use your own words, which suit you better: the claim is not only blasphemous but the height of madness. Men demand that the words of the Spirit give account of themselves, and they profess to be disciples of the Gospels while rising up against those very Gospels. See how precisely and clearly the divine words bear witness to the Son's generation before the ages. Matthew became the narrator of the generation according to the flesh, as he himself says: "The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David." Mark made the preaching of John the beginning of the Gospel, saying, "The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet: A voice of one crying in the wilderness." Luke too approached theology through bodily beginnings. So the evangelist John, who came last to writing, had to lift his mind above everything perceptible and above the time that goes with such things. Or rather, he was raised up by the power of the Spirit and approached him who is beyond all things. He all but protested, like the Apostle, that even if we have known Christ according to the flesh, we know him so no longer. Taking hold of the beginning itself, and leaving all bodily and temporal notions below his own theology, he outsounded the earlier proclamations by the grandeur of his knowledge. The beginning, he says, is not from Mary, nor from these times. What then? "In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God." In these few words he embraced it all: the eternal existence, the impassible generation, the oneness of nature with the Father, the majesty of the nature. By adding "was" he carried it back to the beginning, as if stopping the mouths of those who blaspheme that "he was not," and cutting off from afar any entry for such sophisms. Then, having impressed through his theology a vivid outline, as it were, of the nature of the Only-begotten, he points him out with his words, as though to people who already know him: "He was in the beginning with God." Here again, by adding "was," he joins the generation of the Only-begotten to the eternity of the Father. And again: "He was life, and the life was the light of men," and "He was the true light." Yet although the statement is secured on every side by these additions that signify eternity, he thrusts aside all the testimonies of the Spirit, and seems not even to hear the Spirit crying out "was" to us so often,

"Not being," he says, "he was begotten." Then he was begotten later, as an addition. But if he was not this in the beginning, as you claim, what clearer conflict could anyone point to with the words of the Gospels in which we have believed? 16. And surely every sensible person would agree with this: just as the eye, when it falls away from places full of light, necessarily [?] ceases its activity for lack of light, so too the mind, when it forces its way by imaginings to what lies outside being, becomes confused as though the light of truth were failing it, loses its understanding, and stops thinking. The eye cannot use its sight outside the light, and neither can the soul use its thought once it has been carried away from the conception of the Only-begotten. For falling away from the truth is the mind's sightlessness and blindness. So [?] the mind ... and is blinded, truly knowing nothing, when it imagines it has grasped things older than the Only-begotten. It is as if someone were to praise the sharp sight of an eye that stares into darkness. For "in your light," it says, "we shall see light." But whoever claims to have come to grasp the time when the light did not yet exist is in the same state as those in a frenzied delirium who imagine they see things that are not there. For nothing above the Son can be conceived. What perceptible light is to the eye, God the Word is to the soul. For "there was," it says, "the true light, which enlightens every man coming into the world." So a soul without light is incapable of thought. How then could you grasp what lies above the begetting of the light? Those who care even a little for the truth ought, I think, to let go of bodily likenesses and stop soiling their conceptions of God with material imaginings. They ought to follow the teachings about God handed down to us by the Holy Spirit. Instead of these questions, which are no better than riddles and carry danger whichever answer one assumes, they should conceive a begetting worthy of God: impassible, without partition, undivided and timeless. They should be led to the divine begetting by the radiance that shines forth from light. And they should conceive the image of the invisible God, not after the manner of man-made [?] (variant: the second manuscript reads "one might point to"; two other manuscripts read [?])

images that are fashioned later, after the archetype, but as coexisting and subsisting alongside the prototype that gave it being [?]. It was not stamped out by imitation, as though the whole nature of the Father had been impressed on the Son as on a seal. Or, if you like, it is like the substance of the arts, which passes whole from teachers into learners: the teachers lack nothing, and the learners gain perfection. Or rather, this is not an exact likeness, because it takes an extension of time. It is more fitting to say that it is like the nature of thoughts, which coexist timelessly with the movements of the mind. 17. And let no one slander my argument if some of the examples do not fit the matter in every respect. Small and paltry things cannot be fitted exactly to divine and eternal ones. They serve only to refute the dissembling of those who cannot grasp in thought a begetting without passion. The Son is called, and is, a begotten image. He is the radiance of God's glory, and the wisdom, power and righteousness of God, not as a habit or an aptitude but as a living and active substance, and he is the radiance of God's glory. That is why he shows the whole Father in himself, since he has shone forth from the whole of the Father's glory. To say that the glory of God has no radiance, or that the wisdom of God was ever not with God, is surely the height of absurdity. "But if he was," he says, "he was not begotten." Let us answer, then, that since he was begotten, he was. He does not have his being as an unbegotten one, but he always is and is with the Father, from whom he also has the cause of his existence. When, then, was he brought into being by the Father? From the time the Father is? "But the Father is from eternity," he says. Then the Son too is from eternity, joined in a begotten way to the Father's unbegottenness. To show that this argument is not our own, we will set before them the very words of the Holy Spirit. From (variants: "subsisting alongside the prototype that gave it being, the archetype being [?]"; Regius [?] "subsisting alongside that which, under the prototype, gave it being [?]"; others "to the prototype that gave it being" [?] ... editions [?]; more recent "to the prototype that gave it being" [?]. Regius 4 reads "Father, from whom also".)

the Gospel let us take "In the beginning was the Word", and from the psalm, spoken as though in the person of the Father, "From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you." Putting the two together, let us say that he both was and was begotten. "I have begotten" signifies the cause from which he has the beginning of his being; "was" signifies his timeless existence before the ages. But he, fighting on for his own deception, thinks he can lead the argument into absurdity. EUNOMIUS: "For if the Son was before his own begetting, he was unbegotten." BASIL: But this "before the begetting", you fool, is either something wholly non-existent, a fabrication of the mind resting on no subject (and why argue with senseless people? it would be like quarrelling with someone whose reason has been deranged by frenzy), or else, if it refers to something that exists, it will be carried back to the notion of the ages. But if all the ages are conceived as lying somewhere below the begetting of the Only-begotten, since they are his works, then whoever looks for what is older than the Son's subsistence is wasting his effort. He is asking nothing different than if he were to inquire about the Father too, whether he existed before his own constitution or not. There it is a senseless question to seek something higher than the one who is without beginning and unbegotten. Here too, in the case of him who is with the Father from eternity and has nothing between himself and the one who begot him, it is truly equal folly to ask temporal questions about "before". It is like asking what will happen after the death of the immortal, and inquiring what existed before the begetting of the eternal. But because the Father's beginninglessness is called eternal, they declare the eternal to be the same as the beginningless; and since the Son is not unbegotten, they do not confess that he is eternal either. Yet these differ greatly in meaning. "Unbegotten" is said of that which has no beginning of itself and no cause of its being; "eternal" is said of that which in its being is older than all time and every age. Hence the Son is both not unbegotten and eternal. Some even think the ages worthy of the name "eternal", as having received this title from "always being" [aei einai]. But we consider it the same derangement both to attribute eternity to creation and the (two ancient books read "morning star, I today"; Regius 4 reads "the asking"; the editions read "some ... of eternal", but the manuscripts read "of the eternal".)

BASIL: Who is so ambitious in piety? Who has ever prided himself on loving Christ as much as these men exult in words of insult and dishonour that tear down the glory of the Only-begotten? Will you not stop, godless man, calling non-existent him who truly is, the fountain of life, who grants being to all that exists? In his oracle to his own servant Moses he found a name proper to himself and fitting his eternity, naming himself "He who is". For "I am," he says, "he who is." And no one will deny that these words were spoken in the person of the Lord, no one at least who does not have the Jewish veil lying over his own heart at the reading of Moses. For it is written that an angel of the Lord appeared to Moses in the bush in a flame of fire. Having placed the angel at the head of the narrative, Scripture then introduces the voice of God: "He said," it says, "to Moses: I am the God of your father Abraham"; and shortly afterwards again: "I am he who is." Who, then, is at once angel and God? Is it not the one of whom we have learned that his name is called Angel of Great Counsel? I do not think more is needed to prove it. For lovers of Christ a reminder is enough, while the incurable will gain nothing from a multitude of words. Even if he became Angel of Great Counsel later, he did not disdain the name of angel before then either. For this is not the only place where we find our Lord called both angel and God by Scripture. Jacob too, recounting the vision to his wives, says: "And the angel of God said to me"; and shortly afterwards, from the same one: "I am the God who appeared to you in the place where you anointed a pillar to me." Yet there, at the pillar, it was said to Jacob: "I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father, and the God of Isaac." So the one who is called angel here says there that he was manifested (some books read "had come to be", and so also [?]; Regius 4 reads "insult and impiety"; [?] third reads "might exult ... of the Only-begotten"; the editions and two manuscripts read "in the person of God"; [?] books "his own"; the editions and our manuscripts read "in a flame of fire"; soon after follows "where you anointed to me" [?])

to Jacob. It is clear to everyone, then, that wherever the same one is called both angel and God, it is the Only-begotten who is meant. He manifested himself to men in each generation and announced the Father's will to his saints. So in the case of Moses too, the one who named himself "He who is" can be understood as none other than God the Word, who was in the beginning with God. 19. But those who speak unrighteousness on high have not shrunk from calling the Son non-existent. "The fool said in his heart, There is no God"; but these men did not merely think it. They spoke it in wickedness and did not refuse to hand it down in writing to later times, daring to call God non-existent. And since they see that not even the demons deny that God exists, they go back in their argument to the time before, and there they fulfil their impious desire. They blaspheme that the Son once was not, as being non-existent by his own nature and brought into being by God through grace. Paul uttered a word about idols, saying, "You were slaves to those that by nature are not gods"; and Jeremiah said, "And they swore by those that are not gods"; and the most wise Esther said, "Do not hand over your sceptre, Lord, to those that are not." These men have said this very thing of the true God; how could they still rightly claim the name of Christians? For elsewhere too this same Apostle, speaking in the Spirit of God, calls the Gentiles "things that are not" because they were deprived of the knowledge of God, saying, "God chose the things that are not." ... For since God is "He who is", and truth and life, those who (the editions read "So also in", but two manuscripts read "So also he who in"; [?] the editions afterwards read "that there is not"; the word "that" [?]; "blaspheming God": the older codices read "the Son".)

have handed down, and we too have found it in the writings. But he would not consent to grant our God even the name in which the servants of Christ share. Instead he called non-existent the one who brought creation from non-being into being. One can see his contempt still more clearly from the very ways in which he pretends to exalt the Lord. EUNOMIUS: "We do not make the substance of the Only-begotten common with the things that came into being from what is not, since what is not is not a substance. Rather, we assign him as much superiority as the maker must have over his own works." BASIL: Having brought his argument to this point by his constructions, he plays the benefactor with his phrase and says that he does not make the substance of the Only-begotten common with things that came from what is not. Yet if the God of all, because he is unbegotten, necessarily differs from begotten things, and all begotten things share a subsistence from what is not, how are they not necessarily joined in nature? There, unapproachability separates the natures; here, equality of honour brings them together into one. They say that the Son and the things made by him are from what is not, and in this respect they make their nature common; yet they say they do not grant him a substance like that of the things from what is not. Again, he speaks as though he himself were lord to grant the Only-begotten as much dignity as he pleases: "For we assign him," he says, "as much superiority as the maker must have over his own works." He did not say "we have grasped" or "we believe", as was fitting in speaking of God, but "we assign", as though he himself controlled the measure of the distribution. And how much superiority does he give? "As much," he says, "as the maker must have over his own works." That does not yet testify to any difference of substance. For men surpass their own works in skill, yet they are of the same substance as them, as the potter is with the clay and the shipbuilder with the timber. Both alike are bodies, both alike perceptible, both earthly. 20. Having conceded the Son only this much difference from creation, he now corrupts the very notion of "Only-begotten". EUNOMIUS: "For he is Only-begotten," he says, "because, having been begotten and created alone by the only one through the power of the unbegotten, he became a most perfect minister." (One codex reads "to exalt the Son". One codex reads "to exalt the Son". [?] manuscripts read "from things that are not".)

BASIL: I do not know which of his statements deserves more indignation. Should it be the knavery he practised on the name "Only-begotten", taking its meaning against both human usage and the pious tradition of the Scriptures? (For in common usage "only-begotten" means not one begotten by one alone, but one who alone was begotten.) Or should it be the blasphemy of "creature", which he deliberately joined to "begotten"? He did this to show that the Lord shares the title of "begotten" in no way differently from creatures. On his view, just as it is said, "I have begotten and raised up sons," and "Israel is my firstborn son," so too the Lord has been named Son. He does not have the name above every name; he has merely been granted the title on an equal footing with others. They take refuge in Solomon's phrase, and from there, as from a base of operations, they make raids on the faith. Because "The Lord created me" was spoken in the person of Wisdom, they suppose they are entitled to call the Lord a creature. I have much I could say about this phrase. First, it is said only once in all the Scriptures. Second, it occurs in a book whose meaning is largely hidden and which is set out mostly in proverbs, parables, dark sayings and riddles, so that nothing indisputable or clear can be drawn from it. But I pass over this, so as not to lengthen my discourse with longer digressions, especially since we have postponed to its proper place our examination of the passages they have misunderstood. There, God granting, this part too will be set right. And I think (let it be said with God's help) that a far more consistent meaning of this phrase, one that carries no danger, will come to light on examination. For the moment, though, let us not leave this point unremarked either: other translators, who have grasped more aptly the meaning (the fifth and sixth read "since alone from alone by the [power] of the"; "before his works, The Lord possessed me"; "from alone", absurdly [?]; the editions read "lengthen; but so that also in its own".)

of the Hebrew words, have rendered "acquired me" instead of "created". This will be the greatest obstacle to their blasphemy of "creature". For she who said, "I have acquired a man through God," evidently used this word not because she had created Cain but because she had given birth to him. 21. But let us return to where we began. EUNOMIUS: "He is Only-begotten," he says, "because, having been begotten and created by the only one, he became most perfect."

BASIL: If, then, he is called Only-begotten not because he alone was begotten but because he is from the only one, and if by your account being created is the same as being begotten, why do you not also call him "only-created", you who so easily think and utter anything at all? On our account, it seems, no human being is only-begotten, since everyone is born from a pairing. Nor was Sarah the mother of an only-begotten child, since she did not bear him alone but with Abraham. If your views prevail, we must relearn all our usage, so that the name means not the absence of brothers but the lack of co-parents. And then creation too falls short in dignity of its cause, God the Word, missing out on being only-begotten itself just to the extent that the Son took part with the Father in the work of creation. Yet they do not concede even this, for they call him a most perfect minister. How then, on your account, has creation too not come into being from the only one, since you attach God the Word to the Father like some lifeless instrument? Unless someone is going to deny that the shipbuilder alone made the ship because he used tools to build it! So creation is only-begotten too, and so are its parts: not only the invisible powers but also perceptible bodies, even the meanest of them, gnats and locusts and frogs. For he himself spoke, and they came to be. What ministry would he need who creates by will alone, when creation comes to subsist together with his willing? But what then? How, on our account, are all things through the Son? Because the divine will, setting out as from a fountain, from the first cause, through the (the editions read "the same"; the old books read "the same" [different form]. The Paris edition reads "not even this 'to take part' by them", [?] having added "to take part" from a codex [?]. The editions read "But surely how?"; but the manuscripts read "But what? How?")

proper image, God the Word, goes forth into action. But he called the only-begotten Son a minister, and added as a great tribute that he is well suited to carrying out what he is commanded. Yet if his glory lies not in being perfect God but in being an exact minister, how will he differ from the ministering spirits, who blamelessly perform the work of their service? That is why he joined "created" to "begotten": so that from this too he might show that there is no difference between Son and creature. 22. It is worth hearing his exhortation as well. EUNOMIUS: "We must not attend to the names Father and Son and think of his begetting in a human way, nor be led by human generations to subject God to the names and passions of participation." BASIL: The exhortation means that one must not think of a likeness in substance between Son and Father. That is what his prohibition of "participation" is meant to convey: that the Father's substance has nothing in common with the substance of the Only-begotten. That is the reason for those solemn distinctions between names, the mass of which we have passed over: that things expressed by the same words are not thereby the same in what they signify. His aim is to take away from God his being Father of the Son, on the grounds that men on earth are called fathers. But although many things separate Christianity from Greek error and Jewish ignorance, I think there is no doctrine in the Gospel of our salvation more decisive than faith in the Father and the Son. For even those who have split off into every kind of error agree that God is creator and maker. But what of one who proclaims a Father falsely so called and a Son in bare title only, and thinks it makes no difference whether one confesses a Father or a creator, or says Son or work? Where shall we place him? To which portion shall he be counted, that of the Jews or that of the Greeks? He will certainly not enrol himself among the Christians, since he denies the power of piety and, as it were, the distinctive mark of our worship. For we did not believe in a maker and a work; we were sealed into the Father and the Son through the grace given in baptism. So whoever dares to reject these words sets aside at one stroke the whole power of the Gospels, not ... a Father (the old books read "and Son"; the editions read "and of the Son"; [?] manuscripts read "for these reasons".)

Against Eunomius, Book II. … [a Father who has not] begotten, and proclaiming a Son who has not been begotten. "But I say this," he says, "to avoid the notion of passion that comes with the word 'Father.'" Surely, though, a man who had learned to be pious ought to have rejected whatever was incongruous in the sense of these words, if there was in fact anything of the kind. He should not have thrown out the whole word at once, nor, on the excuse that part of it was unfitting, discarded along with it everything useful in it. Instead he should have kept the doctrines about God clean of lowly and carnal ideas, and conceived of a begetting that befits the holiness and impassibility of God. He should have left aside the manner in which God begot as ineffable and beyond comprehension, but let the term "begetting" guide him to likeness in essence. And yet anyone who looks into it will see that these names, I mean "father" and "son," do not by their nature properly and primarily produce a notion of bodily passions. Said by themselves, they indicate only their relation to one another. A father is one who has given another the beginning of being in a nature like his own; a son is one who has received the beginning of his being from another by way of begetting. 25. So when we hear that a man is a father, we also take in the notion of passion. But when we hear that God is Father, our reasoning goes back to the impassible cause. This man, however, has grown used to this name in the case of a nature subject to passion, and so he denies as impossible whatever lies beyond the grasp of his own reasoning. It is not right to look at the passion of corruptible things and then disbelieve the impassibility of God. Nor is it right to set the unchangeable and unalterable essence beside a nature that is in flux and subject to countless changes. And because mortal animals beget through passion, one should not think the same of God. One should rather be led from this toward the truth: since corruptible things beget in this way, the incorruptible begets in the opposite way. Nor could he say that these names are properly and primarily assigned to human beings, and that we apply them to God loosely. For our Lord Jesus Christ, leading us back to the beginning of all things and the true cause of what exists, says: "Call no one on earth your father, for you have one Father, who is in heaven." How then can he demand that we discard these words as primarily indicating fleshly passions, when the Lord transfers them from human beings to Him as befitting the impassibility of God? And if

he is also called Father of creatures, this still does not conflict with our argument. He who "has begotten the drops of dew," as Job puts it, did not beget the drops and the Son in the same way. If they dare to say that he did, and so to give the substance of dew the name "son" on an equal footing, they will release us from all further argument with them, since they will have pushed their blasphemy to the most open shamelessness. Not even when God is called Father of us all is he Father of us and of the Only-begotten in the same way. And if the fact that the Lord is called "firstborn of all creation" and "firstborn among many brothers" trains them in impiety, let them learn from the Gospel that the Lord calls those who have become his kin by works of virtue his mother and his brothers. "For who is my mother," he says, "and who are my brothers, but those who do the will of my Father in heaven?" So God is called our Father not loosely or by metaphor, but properly, primarily and truly. Through our bodily parents he has brought us into being out of non-being, and by his care he makes us his own. And if we say that God is truly called the Father of us, who have been counted worthy of the grace of adoption, what argument will deny that the Son by nature, who came forth from his essence, may fittingly call him Father? EUN. "One must not," he says, "conceive the Lord's generation in a human way because of the names Father and Son." BAS. I say so too. But what prevents the pious from believing in a divine and impassible generation? I think, though, that he uses these words to show not that God begot impassibly, but that he did not beget at all. How then, my good man, did you declare in your earlier arguments that the essence of the Only-begotten is an offspring? If he has not been begotten, how by your own argument could being an offspring belong to him? But because of the opposition of the begotten to the unbegotten, he was eager to show that the essence is an offspring;

but now, seeing that this word also signifies kinship of essence, he takes the fact of having been begotten away from the offspring. And yet if he rejects this as indicating passion, what prevents him from refusing, for the same reasons, to accept that God is Creator? With every bodily activity some labor, greater or less, is always joined, in proportion to the power of the maker and the differences in the size of the things produced. [?] Yet to say that the divine and blessed nature is gripped by toil is no less impious than to subject it to the most shameful passions. [?] But if he creates without passion, accept that the begetting too is without passion. 24. [?] It has now been shown well enough that God is properly and fittingly called Father, and that this is a name not of passion but of kinship, whether by grace, as with human beings, or by nature, as with the Only-begotten. [?] But let us grant that this word too is figurative and used by metaphor, like countless others. [?] When we hear that God is angry, or sleeps, or flies, and other such things that make an unfitting impression at first glance, we neither strike out the words of the Spirit nor take what is said in a bodily sense. [?] Why then, when this word has been used so constantly by the Spirit, do we not search out its meanings that are fitting to God? [?] Or shall we erase this one word alone from Scripture, slandering it on the basis of human usage? [?] Let us look at it this way. In ordinary usage here below, the term "beget" signifies two things: the passion of the one who begets, and his kinship with the one begotten. [?] So when the Father says to the Only-begotten, "From the womb before the morning star I begot you," and, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you," which shall we say the word presents: the passion of those who beget, or the kinship of nature? [?] I say the latter, and I do not think even these people would contradict it unless they had been carried off into outright madness. [?] So if the word is proper to God, why do you dishonor it as foreign? But if it has been carried over from human things, pick out what is sound in it and shun the worse of its meanings. [?] Surely, with a word of many meanings, one may be guided by the word to the right notion and pass beyond what is lowly in its connotation. [?] And do not say to me, "What is (84) The editions read εἶναι δεικνύναι; five old books read οὖσαν δεικνύναι. Shortly after, some manuscripts read φιλονεικεῖ. [?] … ἐκ μεταφορᾶς [?]

the begetting? Of what kind is it, and how could it come about?" The manner is entirely ineffable and beyond comprehension, but that is no reason for us to cast away the firm faith in Father and Son. If we were going to measure everything by our own comprehension, and suppose that whatever reason cannot grasp does not exist at all, then the reward of faith would be gone, and the reward of hope gone too. How could we still be worthy of the blessings laid up for faith in things unseen, if we trusted only what is evident to reason? Why did the nations "become futile, and their senseless heart was darkened"? Was it not because they followed what seemed right to their own reasoning and disobeyed the preaching of the Spirit? And whom does Isaiah lament as lost? "Woe to those who are wise in themselves and knowing in their own sight." Is it not people like these? (91) … and not a few manuscripts read ἐκ τῶν λογισμῶν. (93) The editions read παραδεχθῆναι αὐτό. The ancient books [?]. (94) The editions and two manuscripts read μόνον τοῖς παρατεθεῖσιν; [?] παρατεθεῖσιν. For that ἐπισημηνάμενος [?] something [?]

EUN. "If they cared at all for the truth, they ought to confess that since the names are different, the essences are different too." BAS. Could anyone use words more carelessly? Within a short space he turns to the opposite position. Now he says that a difference of names necessarily indicates a difference of essences, and now again that a sharing of names does not make the essences common. But I think we are doing something like those who convict a man of murder on the evidence of an insult, or a blow, or some offense of that kind. 25. Let us move on, then, to the chief of his evils. All Christians alike, at least those truly worthy of the name, share a common conviction: that the Son is begotten light, shining forth from the unbegotten light, and that he is life itself and goodness itself, proceeding from the life-giving source of the Father's goodness. This man saw that, and then realized that unless he could shake these convictions of ours, his sophisms would gain him nothing more. Anyone who confesses that the Father is light, and that the Son is light as well, will be led of his own accord to confess kinship of essence, since the notion of light is one and the same. Between light and light, by the very definition of light, there is no difference, either in how it is spoken or in the notion itself. So to take this away from us, he wraps the doctrine of the faith in nets of trickery. He teaches that these are utterly incomparable and have nothing in common with each other, and says that the same opposition that exists between unbegotten and begotten exists also between light and light. Otherwise, if we shrink from this, he forces us to confess that God is composite. But let us rather hear his own words. EUN. "Does 'light' signify something different in the case of the unbegotten than in the case of the begotten, or is it the same in each? If it is one thing in one case and another in the other, then clearly what is put together from one thing and another is composite, and the composite is not unbegotten. But if it is the same, then as far as the begotten differs from the unbegotten, so far must light differ from light, and life from life, and power from

BAS. See and understand how horrifying this impiety is. "As far," he says, "as the unbegotten differs from (99) Οὐδὲν αὐτῷ πλέον τῶν σοφισμάτων. Translate [?] … For confessing the Father as light … οἰκειότητος ὑπ-[?] Let ταυτότητος (identity) be read in place of οἰκειότητος (kinship). It makes little difference.

the begotten, so far will light differ from light, and life from life, and power from power." Let us ask him, then: by what measure is the unbegotten set apart from the begotten? By some small measure, so small that the two might at some point coincide? Or is that completely impossible, even more impossible than for the same person to be alive and dead at once, healthy and sick at the same time, awake and asleep together? All things set against each other in extreme opposition are like this: when one is present, the other must be absent, and by nature they can never exist together or coincide. 26. Since, then, the unbegotten is opposed to the begotten in this way, consider the man who calls the Father light and the Son light too, but says that this light is as far from that light as the begotten is from the unbegotten. Even if in words he pretends to be generous, calling the Son "light" forsooth, is he not plainly leading the idea toward its opposite by the force of what he says? Consider: what is opposed to the unbegotten, another unbegotten or the begotten? The begotten, obviously. And what is opposed to light, another light or darkness? Darkness, certainly. If, then, as far as the begotten differs from the unbegotten, so far must light differ from light, who could fail to see the impiety? Under the name of light you bring in what is opposed to light, and you insinuate that the essence of the Only-begotten is contrary to the nature of light. Otherwise, let him show us a light opposed to light, with the same measure of opposition that the begotten has to the unbegotten. And if no such thing exists, and he could not even conceive of it himself, then let us not overlook the art with which he builds his blasphemy deep down. Because he thinks the begotten is opposed to the unbegotten as its contrary, he applies the same opposition to light and light, so as to show in every respect that the essence of the Father is the adversary and enemy of the essence of the Only-begotten. That is the reason for this new legislation of doctrine: "As far as the begotten differs from the unbegotten, so far must light differ from light." And yet between the unbegotten and the begotten there is a certain [opposition], according to the positing of the (8) The editions read ἀλλὰ τῇ δυνάμει. The second Regius reads ἀλλ' αὐτῇ γε τῇ δυν. Another manuscript reads ἀλλὰ τῇ γε δυν. [?] (9) Εἰ δὲ τοῦτο οὔτε ἔστι φῶς, etc.

have the same conflict with one another as the antecedents have; and when one of two contraries has its contrary, the contrary will certainly follow the other as well. For example, if light goes with sight, darkness goes with blindness; if perception goes with being alive, lack of perception goes with being dead. But anyone who pays even a little attention knows that this rule is weak and breaks down. Life goes with being awake, but it does not follow that death goes with being asleep. Nor, in fact, is the begotten contrary to the unbegotten. If they were contraries, they would destroy each other, and may that recoil on the heads of the blasphemers! But they are not hostile by nature, and what follows from them will not necessarily have the same separation that the antecedents were shown to have. 27. So either erase your words, or do not deny the impiety. The blasphemy is yours, for you are the one who said: "As far as the unbegotten differs from the begotten, so far must light differ from light." Then, just as the begotten will never share in unbegottenness, so you will never let him share in light. And by your account the essence of the Only-begotten will be just as far from being conceived and named light as it is from being unbegotten. John, with the mighty voice of the Spirit, cries out to you, saying: "He was the true light." But you have no ears to hear and no heart to understand. Instead, with your sophisms you drive the essence of the Only-begotten toward the nature that opposes light and cannot exist alongside it. You will not offer as a strong point that you did not take the name of light away from the Only-begotten. Piety does not lie in a noise in the air, but in the force of what is meant. He did not stop there, either. He drags life and power along too, by the same measure of departure toward the contrary, saying: "As far as the begotten differs from the unbegotten, so far must light differ from light, and life from life, and power from power." So by your account the Only-begotten is neither life nor power. Then you will strike out the Lord himself when he says, "I am the life," and you will strike out Paul when he says, "Christ the power of God." What was shown above will apply here as well. No one would say that life or power is opposed to life and power. Death and powerlessness make up the complete opposition. All of this he, in

his craftiness, hides as a deceit in words, and so he builds the horror of his impiety deep down and under cover. By the tricks of his words he moves the nature of the Only-begotten off to the opposite of the Father, and leaves nothing but the fair sound of the names. What then shall we say? How shall we, who confess that the Father is unbegotten and the Son begotten, escape a contrariety in their very being? By saying what? That the Son of a good Father is good; that from the unbegotten light the eternal light shone forth; that from the true life the life-giving source came forth; and that from power itself the power of God appeared. Darkness, death and weakness are ranked with the ruler of this world, the world-rulers of darkness, the spiritual forces of wickedness, and every power hostile to the divine nature. Even these were not allotted their opposition to the good in their very essence (for then the blame would go back to the Creator). They slid away into evil by their own choice, through privation of the good. Yet this God-fighting tongue has tried to bring the nature of the Only-begotten into this very rank. He cannot claim that he made the essence of the Father a light surpassing in glory and brightness, and supposed that of the Only-begotten to be light too, only somewhat dimmer and, as it were, clouded. Even that would not come from a pious mind, for the dimness of the image would take away its likeness. Still, we could only have wished that this was the charge against him, for then we would not need much of a struggle to set him right.
