the unbegotten is not an intensification of the begotten, nor is the begotten some diminution of the unbegotten; the distance between them is, as it were, diametrical. Those who make "begotten" and "unbegotten" the essence will be faced with these absurdities and still more. The contrary will have been begotten from its contrary, and instead of natural kinship, a strife that is necessary and lies in the essence itself will come to light for them. To say that one essence is contrary to any other essence whatever shows ignorance even more than impiety. It was agreed long ago, even among the wise men outside the faith, that contrariety cannot exist in essence. (These people treat those wise men as worthless whenever they do not find them supporting their blasphemies.) But suppose one accepts what is true: that "begotten" and "unbegotten" are distinguishing properties observed in the essence, which lead us by the hand to a clear and unconfused notion of Father and Son. Then one will escape the danger of impiety and keep one's reasoning consistent. Properties are like marks and shapes observed in the essence. They divide what is common by their distinctive marks, but they do not cut through the essence's sameness of nature. For example, the Godhead is common, while fatherhood and sonship are particular properties. From the combination of the two, the common and the particular, we come to grasp the truth. So when we hear "unbegotten light" we think of the Father, and when we hear "begotten light" we form the notion of the Son. As light and light, there is no contrariety between them; as begotten and unbegotten, the opposition is observed. This is the nature of properties: to show otherness within identity of essence. The properties themselves are often set against one another and stand apart as contraries, yet they do not tear apart the unity of the essence. Think of winged and footed, aquatic and terrestrial, rational and irrational. A single essence underlies them all, and these properties do not make the essence foreign to itself or provoke it, as it were, into faction against itself. Instead, by the working of these distinguishing marks, they kindle a kind of light in our souls and guide us to such understanding as our minds can reach. But this man transfers the opposition of the properties to the essence, and from there he draws his occasion for impiety, frightening us like children with sophisms (27) The editions read οὐδὲ ἀνάπαλιν τό. Five old books read οὐδὲ μὴν τό. [?] τοῦτο δὲ καὶ πλείω. [?] καί in five manuscripts.

[?] that if light were something other than the unbegotten, God will necessarily be shown by us to be composite. 29. And what do I say? That if light were not something other than the unbegotten, it could no longer be said of God in the way it is, any more than the unbegotten itself can. One could learn the difference between what these words signify from this as well. God is said to dwell in light and to put on light as a garment, but Scripture nowhere says that he dwells in his own unbegottenness, or has it wrapped around himself from outside (such things would indeed be laughable). Begotten and unbegotten, rather, are certain distinguishing properties. For if there were nothing to mark out the substance, it would in no way get through to our understanding. Since the Godhead is one, it is impossible to form a distinct notion of the Father or of the Son unless our thought is articulated by the addition of the properties. As for the claim that God will turn out to be composite if light is not taken to be the same as the unbegotten, we can say this. If we took the unbegotten as a part of the substance, the argument would have some force, since it says that whatever is made up of different things is composite. But suppose we hold that the substance of God is light, or life, or the good, he being wholly life in what he is, and wholly light, and wholly good, while the life has the unbegotten as an attendant feature. Then how is he who is simple in substance not incomposite? Surely the modes that point out his property will not disturb the principle of his simplicity. Otherwise everything that is said about God will show us that God is composite. And it seems that if we mean to preserve the notion of what is simple and without parts, either we shall say nothing about God except "unbegotten", and refuse to call him invisible, incorruptible, unchangeable, creator, judge, and all the other names we now use in giving him glory; or else, accepting these names, what are we to do? Shall we take them all and store them up in the substance? Then we shall show him to be not only composite but made up of unlike parts, since each of these names signifies something different. Or shall we take them as outside the substance? Then whatever account they devise for each of those names… [Note 55: The fourth Royal manuscript reads ἀναγκαίως σύνθετος ὁ Θεὸς ἡμῶν ἀποδειχθήσεται. Note 56: The editions read ἔννοιαν ἰδιάζουσαν; the manuscripts read ἰδιάζουσαν ἔννοιαν.]
[Note 57: The phrase μὴ … τῆς διανοίας διαρθρουμένης is read thus [?]… and the sixth manuscript reads ἀγαθὸν ὅλον ὥσπερ ἐστὶ ζωὴν ὄντα, without [?]]

…let them show that the same account holds for the title "unbegotten" too. 30. Having filled his treatise with empty drivel, and set himself up above everyone who has ever devoted himself to the knowledge of God, as if he alone had cut some new and fresh road leading to God that none of his predecessors discovered, at last he brings in his blasphemy against the Son, as though the very substance of God had taught it to him. EUN. That the [substance] which is above kingship and wholly incapable of generation, teaching by these things the mind that approaches with goodwill, bids it by a law of nature to thrust as far away as possible any comparison with another. BAS. Does he not plainly show that he himself was found worthy of the revelation of things unspeakable, since he brought his mind to God with goodwill? And for this reason he thrusts the Only-begotten as far as possible from fellowship with the Father, not even thinking him fit to be admitted to comparison. He even says that by a law of nature the substance of the Only-begotten has been marked off from that of the Father. What does he mean by this? That the God of the universe could not admit the Only-begotten to kinship of substance even if he wished, because a law of nature barred him from union with him. It seems he is not his own master but is yoked under the bounds of necessity. For that is what things held fast by the law of nature are like: they are led, without choosing it, to whatever their nature decrees. Fire heats by nature, not by choice, and is necessarily incapable of receiving cold, since the law of nature has deprived it of any fellowship with cold. In the same way he would have God the Father too hold a substance estranged from the Son by a law of nature. And yet… [Note 42: The editions read Ἐμπλήσας καὶ τόν; five manuscripts read Ἐμπλήσας δὲ τόν. Note 43: The Paris edition reads Ὅτι ἡ μὲν ἀνωτέρω βασιλεία. It should be [?] in this way: Ἡ μὲν οὐσία ἀνωτέρω βασι[λείας] … δεδιδαγμένος τοῦ Θεοῦ τῆς οὐσίας, [?] itself.]

…the laws of nature do not separate the Son from the Father. Rather, they make their fellowship necessary and unbreakable. Suppose he had said that the God of the universe had by his own will made himself incommunicable. Even then, the account of God's goodness would not allow it to be credible that the Father shares none of what is his with the one who is from him; but at least his words would have been consistent. To say, however, that the estrangement exists by a law of nature is the mark of someone who has not even examined the nature found in sensible things. By that nature it is not what is alien or contrary that each thing begets, but rather what is akin and fitting to it. 31. Here again, then, he has failed to notice that his statements contradict each other. For in [?], in his indignation against those who say that the Only-begotten is like the Father in substance, he wrote this: EUN. To begin with, those who have dared to compare the substance that has no master, which is superior to every cause and free of all laws, with the begotten substance that is subject to paternal laws seem to me either never to have examined the nature of the universe at all, or to make their judgments about these matters with a mind that is not pure. BAS. How, then, has the substance that has no master and is free of all laws now turned out to hold its incomparability not voluntarily, but because a law of nature has taken hold of it first? How does it drive the begotten from fellowship with itself without choosing to, so that for this reason it is unapproachable even to the Only-begotten himself? So much, then, for the inconsistency of his statements; but how great is their impiety! He calls the Father's substance masterless and free (if indeed what bows to the law of nature has no master), but by contrast he declares the substance of the Only-begotten to be servile, and thereby strips it of equal honor in nature. There are two realities, creation and Godhead. Creation is ranked in servitude and obedience, while Godhead rules and is lord. So whoever strips him of the dignity of lordship and casts him down to the lowliness of servitude is plainly, for that very reason, ranking him with the whole of creation. For it is surely no dignity for him that he will rank ahead of his fellow servants. But unless he were confessed as king and lord, not by a diminution of nature, [?] … [Note 48: [?] … a Royal manuscript reads ἄρρητον κοινωνίαν ποιοῦσιν, "fellowship" [?].]

BAS. He said this to prove that the Only-begotten is estranged from the Father, but it supports our argument. For suppose God's substance gives us to understand that its activity, too, is consistent with and fitting to its own dignity. Then, as Eunomius thinks, the dignity is unbegottenness, and on their account this is also the substance, while the activity of God is the Only-begotten, or the image of the activity. This too is on their account. So it would be pointless to argue against these points, since they have nothing [?]. I would give a great deal for them to disown this blasphemy. But since they have said it, let us draw the conclusion from their own words. If the dignity of God is unbegottenness, and this is also the substance, and the activity is consistent with and fitting to the dignity of God, and in their view this activity is Christ, then he will be proper and fitting to the substance of God. None of this is ours. We simply put their own words together and make the demonstration from them. The dignity, he says, follows on the substance of God; the activity corresponds to the dignity; the Only-begotten is the image of the activity. And in reverse: if the Only-begotten is the image of the activity, and the activity of the dignity, and the dignity of the substance, then the Only-begotten will be the image of the substance. So it often happens that the workers of falsehood themselves, throttled by the force of the truth, bear witness to it even against their will. The demons, too, were not doing the work of evangelists; but since they could not look straight at the light of the truth, they cried out: We know who you are, the [?] of [?]
32. Let us look at what follows. EUN. For whether, he says, someone [?] from the works is led up from them to the substances,
[?] his argument. [?] which I read as ὥς γε τούτοις ἀντιλέγεις οὐκ ἔχουσιν, etc., confirms. —— Καὶ τοῦτο κατά τὸν τούτων λόγον. [?]

…finding the Son a product of the unbegotten, and the Paraclete a product of the Only-begotten, and confirming the difference of activity from the superiority of the Only-begotten, he takes an indisputable proof of the difference in substance as well. BAS. First of all, I for my part do not see how substances can be inferred from works. Products point to power, wisdom and skill, but not to the substance itself. They do not even necessarily display the whole power of the maker, since a craftsman may sometimes not put all his strength into his works, and often uses his skill at less than full stretch. Even if he set his whole power in motion for the work, it would still only be possible to measure his strength through his works, not to grasp his substance, whatever it may be. Suppose instead that, because the divine nature is simple and incomposite, he treats the substance as coinciding with the power. Suppose he says that because of the goodness that belongs to God, the whole power of the Father was set in motion for the begetting of the Son, and again the whole power of the Only-begotten for the existence of the Holy Spirit. Then from the Spirit the power of the Only-begotten would be seen, and with it the substance too; and from the Only-begotten, in turn, the power and substance of the Father would be grasped. Consider what follows from this. The very arguments by which he tried to establish that the substance is unlike turn out to establish its likeness. For if the power has nothing in common with the substance, how were you guided to a grasp of the substance from the works, which are effects of power? But if substance and power are the same, whatever characterizes the power will surely characterize the substance as well. So the works, as you put it, point not to unlikeness of substance but to the exactness of the likeness. Once again this attempt supports our argument rather than his own. Either he can find proof for his statements nowhere, or, if he takes his illustrations from human affairs, he will find that we do not come to understand a craftsman's substance from his works. Rather, we recognize the nature of the begetter from the one he has begotten. For one cannot grasp the substance of the builder from the house [?] … not a product, but a true Son, and [?] … So much for that. [?]

33. And how great a blasphemy is the addition! Despising the threat in the Gospels, which the Lord held out as most terrible to those who blaspheme the Holy Spirit, he calls the Holy Spirit a product. He all but denies that it is even a living being, since this term is mostly applied to lifeless things. That he has already subjected the Lord to this blasphemy is surely no reason for us to relax our indignation in the slightest. It does not excuse the impiety; it adds to the condemnation. For the Lord in his goodness pardoned blasphemy against himself, but declared that those who dared to blaspheme the Holy Spirit could not escape. Of all who have risen up against the truth since the preaching of godliness was proclaimed throughout the world, he is the first to have dared to utter this word about the Spirit. To this day we have not heard anyone call the Holy Spirit a product, nor have we found this term in the writings they left behind. Then he says: EUN. If someone is led up from the works to the comprehension of the substance, he will find the Son a product of the unbegotten, and the Paraclete a product of the Only-begotten. BAS. Here is another kind of impiety: to blaspheme twice in a single phrase, and to take the belittling of the Holy Spirit as agreed, so as to set out from there to prove that the Only-begotten is inferior. It seems that while The heavens declare the glory of God, the Holy Spirit announces the diminishing of the glory of the Only-begotten! And the Lord, speaking of the Paraclete, says, He will glorify me; but this accusing tongue declares that the Spirit stands in the way of the Son's being compared with the Father. For since, he says, the Son is the maker of the Spirit (be merciful to us, Lord, for what is being said!), and the Spirit is such as to add no dignity to the one who made it, the Son is therefore not worthy to be compared with the Father either. The cheapness of what he made [deprives him] of equal rank in dignity

34. Have you ever heard a more grievous blasphemy? Has anyone ever fallen so plainly into the inescapable judgment that awaits blasphemy against the Holy Spirit? [Notes: [?] Καταφρονήσας γάρ. Shortly after, some manuscripts read βλασφημουσ[?]. Note 62: The editions read τινὸς μέχρι σήμερον ἀκηκόαμεν δημιούργημα. Note 63: Two [?] books read τρόπος τῆς βλασφημίας.]

…it belonged to Satan alone to rage so madly against the Spirit: to insult it with lowly names, and to cheapen its nature so far as to say that it brings dishonor on the one who made it. Or rather, even he would have avoided saying anything lowly about the Spirit, so as not to bring down his own pride. But we shall speak of this at leisure. Is it not evident to everyone that no activity of the Son is cut off from the Father, and that nothing in existence belonging to the Son is alien to the Father? For All that is mine is yours, he says, and what is yours is mine. How, then, does he assign the cause of the Spirit to the Only-begotten alone, and treat its creation as a charge against the Son's nature? If he says these things because he sets up two first principles opposed to each other, he will be crushed together with Mani and Marcion. But if he makes all things depend on one principle, then whatever is said to have come into being from the Son is referred to the first cause. So even though we believe that all things were brought into being through God the Word, we do not take away from the God of the universe his being the cause of all. And how can it fail to be plainly dangerous to separate the Spirit from God? On the one hand, the Apostle hands it down to us as joined with both, calling it now the Spirit of Christ and now the Spirit of God, when he writes: If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him; and again: You have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit that is from God. On the other hand, the Lord calls it the Spirit of truth, since he himself is the truth, and says that it proceeds from the Father. But this man, in order to tear down the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ, takes the Spirit away from the Father and assigns it to the Only-begotten in particular, so as to tear down his glory. He heaps insults on him, as he thinks, and expects no punishment for his wicked doctrines on the day of recompense. [Note 65: The editions read ἂν ταπεινῶς; three manuscripts read ἂν τὸ ταπεινῶς. In the same place the editions read μὴ τῦφον ἑαυτοῦ καταβάλλοι. But the fourth Royal manuscript [?] … Ἡμεῖς δὲ … ἐλάβομεν, [?] not Κυρίου … λέγοντος. Translate: "When the Lord [?]". Note 72: The Colbert manuscript, in a second hand, reads ἐφυβρίζων ὡς οἷόν.]

AGAINST EUNOMIUS, ON THE HOLY SPIRIT. 1. BAS. Having at long last had his fill of blasphemies against the Only-begotten, he has passed on to the Holy Spirit, and he discusses the Spirit too in keeping with his whole purpose. He writes this: EUN. Since this much is enough for us about the Only-begotten, it would be fitting to speak next about the Paraclete as well. We do not follow the unexamined opinions of the many, but keep the teaching of the saints in everything. We learned from them that the Spirit is third in dignity and order, and so we have believed that it is third in nature as well. BAS. He does not think one should abide by the simple and unaffected faith of the many, but would rather use artful and sophistical arguments to twist the truth once again to suit his own opinion. What he has said shows this clearly enough. For while he dishonors the opinion of the many, who glorify the Holy Spirit, he pretends to keep the teaching of the saints, and he passes over in silence the people who handed it down to him, now as before. He was shown to be doing the same thing in his arguments about the Only-begotten. Then he says that he learned from the saints that the Spirit is third in order and dignity, but that he believed on his own account that it is also third in nature. Yet he cannot say who these saints are, or in what writings they gave this teaching. Has there ever been a man so bold in introducing innovations into the divine doctrines? For what necessity is there, if the Spirit is third in dignity and order, [Notes: [?] having used his own writings. [?] The fourth and sixth Royal manuscripts read τοῦ αὐτοῦ πρὸς Εὐνόμιον, [?] Spirit. The second Royal manuscript reads "Of the same great Basil, against Eunomius, on the Holy Spirit" [?]. Three manuscripts read ἀκολουθοῦντες … φυλάσσοντες. [A Greek marginal note:] Some say that this treatise is not by St Basil, because certain statements in it seem rather harsh; to whom in nothing it appears [?]]

…for it to be third in nature as well? The account of godliness perhaps hands down that the Spirit is second to the Son in dignity. But we have not been taught by the Holy Scriptures that it has a third nature, nor can this be logically inferred from what was said before. The Son is second to the Father in order, because he is from him; and in dignity, because the Father is the principle and cause by being his Father, and because through the Son we have access and approach to God the Father. But he is not second in nature, because the Godhead in each is one. In just the same way, the Holy Spirit too, even if it ranks below the Son in order and dignity (to concede the point entirely), could not reasonably be held to follow as being of an alien nature [?]. This is clear from the following. All the angels, just as they share one name, so also [?] … [Garbled notes: "For it is second in dignity to the Son, having its being from him, and receiving from him, and announcing to us, and wholly depending on that cause" [?] … in the book, αἰτία τὸ εἶναι αὐτοῦ πατέρα, where see [?] … 16, when he wrote thus, εἶναι τὸ ἀρχέτυπον, [?] … τῷ ἕνα εἶναι τὸν Μονογενῆ, because ὑποβεβηκὸς τόν [?] … also ἵνα καὶ ὅλως συγχωρήσωμεν [?] … It is worth noting that the words Ἀξιώματι μὲν … Note 81: The editions read αἰτία τοῦ εἶναι ὁ Πατήρ. The second Royal manuscript reads αἰτία τὸ εἶναι αὐτοῦ πατέρα. The third Royal manuscript reads αἰτία τοῦ εἶναι πατέρα αὐτοῦ. A Royal manuscript [?] reads αἰτία τῷ ἑνὸς ἑκάστου τὴν προστασίαν πεπιστευμένου. The third Royal and the Colbert manuscripts read ἀγγέλου, τῶν ἑνὸς ἑκάστου τὴν προστασίαν πεπιστευμένων. The second Royal manuscript reads ἀγγέλου, παρὰ τὸν ἑνὸς ἑκάστου τὴν προστασίαν πεπιστευμένον.]

…always behold the face of my Father in heaven. And the Psalmist says: The angel of the Lord will encamp around those who fear him; and: The angel who has delivered me from my youth; and other passages like these. That there are also angels who preside over whole nations, Moses teaches us in his song, where he says: When the Most High divided the nations, when he scattered the sons of Adam, he fixed the boundaries of the nations according to the number of his angels. And wise Daniel, in his vision of the angel, heard him say: The prince of the kingdom of the Persians stood against me; and behold, Michael, one of the chief princes, came to help me, and I left him there with the prince of the king of the Persians. A little later the same angel says: And the prince of the Greeks was coming. There is also one who is called commander-in-chief of the army of the Lord, who appeared to Joshua son of Nun at the Jordan. And again, legions of angels are spoken of, since the Lord said to his disciples: Or do you think that I cannot ask my Father, and he will at once provide me with more than twelve legions of angels? The commander-in-chief, then, is ruler of the angels ranked in the legions

2. What, then, is our argument leading to? To this: it does not follow that whatever is second or third in order and dignity also has a different nature. Among the angels, one is a ruler and another a subject, yet all are angels by nature. The difference lies in dignity, but what they share is their nature. (For Star differs from star in glory, but all stars have one nature; and there are many dwelling places with the Father, that is, differences of dignity, but those who are glorified have a like nature.) In just the same way, the Holy Spirit too, even if it ranks lower in dignity and order, as they say (for we have received it, he says, as numbered third after Father and Son, since the Lord himself handed down this order when he handed down saving baptism, saying: Go, baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit), yet in nature… [Note 87: The editions [?] ἄρχων; many manuscripts read καὶ ὁ ἄρχων. Shortly after, two manuscripts read ἄρχοντος Περσῶν. Our manuscripts read ἢ δοκεῖτε.]

[?] …that it is some third thing, cast out from the Son and the Father, we have learned nowhere. For when two classes of things are spoken of, deity and creation, lordship and servitude, the power that sanctifies and that which is sanctified, that which has virtue by nature and that which achieves it by choice, in which portion shall we rank the Spirit? Among the things that are sanctified? But it is itself sanctification. Among those who acquire virtue by noble deeds? But it is good by nature. Among the ministering beings? But the ministering spirits sent out for service are something else. So it is not lawful to call it our fellow servant, since it is sovereign by nature, nor to number it with creation, since it is numbered with the divine and blessed Trinity. For principalities and powers and all such created beings have their sanctification from attention and diligence, and so could not rightly be called holy by nature. Reaching out for the good, they receive a share of holiness in proportion to their love for God. Iron set in the middle of a fire does not stop being iron, but through its most intense contact with the fire it becomes red-hot, takes the whole nature of the fire into itself, and passes over into fire in both colour and action. In the same way the holy powers, from their communion with what is holy by nature, now have sanctification penetrating their whole substance and grown into their nature. Their difference from the Holy Spirit is this: for the Spirit holiness is its nature, while for them being sanctified comes by participation. And those whose good is acquired and supplied from elsewhere are of a nature that can fall. For Lucifer, who rose in the morning, would not have fallen, nor been crushed upon the earth, if by nature he had been incapable of receiving what is worse. How then can it be pious to rank the Spirit with creation, when it is separated from creation by so great a measure? For creation by its nature has sanctification as the prize of progress and of pleasing God, but it has a self-determining nature, able to incline either way, to choose the good or the worse. The Holy Spirit, however, is the fountain of sanctification. And just as the Father is holy by nature, and the Son is holy by nature, so the Spirit of truth too is holy by nature. That is why [it has] the special and distinctive title of “holy” [?] … (92) Two manuscripts read “numbered among.” [?] … In the same place the third Regius manuscript reads “and to shift the [?] to either…”

…nature? This, I think, is why the Seraphim in Isaiah are recorded as crying out “holy” three times: natural holiness is seen in the three hypostases. And the Spirit shares with the Father and the Son not only the name of holiness but also the very title of “spirit.” For God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth. And the prophet says: “The Spirit before our face, Christ the Lord, of whom we said, In the shadow of his wings we shall live.” And the Apostle applies the title “spirit” to the Lord, saying: “Now the Lord is the Spirit.” From this it is clear to everyone that sharing these names shows not that the Spirit's nature is alien to the Father and the Son but that it is akin to them. God is called good, and he is good; and the Holy Spirit is also good, not having goodness as something acquired but as something that exists with it by nature. Otherwise it would be the most absurd thing of all to say that what is holy by nature does not have its goodness by nature, but as something that supervened and was added to it from outside. And when the Lord said, “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete,” he shows that he himself is also our Paraclete. So the title “Paraclete” too contributes not a little to showing the glory of the Holy Spirit…

4. Such, then, are the names that show the greatness of its nature. And what are the operations of the Holy Spirit? “By the word of the Lord,” it says, “the heavens were made firm, and all their power by the Spirit of his mouth.” So just as God the Word is the creator of the heavens, the Holy Spirit gives the heavenly powers their firmness and stability in virtue. And again Job says: “The Spirit of the Lord, which made me.” He is speaking, I think, not of creation but of being perfected in human virtue. Isaiah, speaking in the person of the Lord (evidently according to his humanity), says: “The Lord has sent me, and his Spirit.” And again the psalm, showing that the power of the Spirit has penetrated everything, says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit, and where shall I flee from your face?” And what kind of benefits reach us from it, and how great are they? Just as the Lord himself

gave those who received him power to become children of God, so too the Holy Spirit is the Spirit of adoption. And just as our Lord is the true teacher, as it is said, “But call no one on earth your teacher, for you have one master, the Christ,” so too the Lord himself testifies that the Holy Spirit teaches all who have believed in the name of the Lord, when he says: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send, he will teach you all things.” And just as the Father is said to distribute the operations to those worthy to receive them, and the Son to distribute the ministries among the ranks of ministry, so too the Holy Spirit distributes the gifts to those worthy to receive them, [as] is testified [?] … 10, 11 [?].

…for God [gives life], as Paul says: “I charge you in the presence of God, who gives life to all things.” And Christ gives life: “My sheep,” he says, “hear my voice, and I give them eternal life.” And we are given life through the Spirit, as Paul says: “He who raised Christ from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.” 5. But this man dares anything. He does not shrink from the danger that hangs over those who dare to hurl a blasphemous word against the Holy Spirit, and he declares that it has no share in deity. He writes this about the Spirit: EUNOMIUS: “Third in order and in nature, brought into being by the command of the Father and the operation of the Son, honoured in the third place as the first and greatest of all and the only such work of the Only-begotten, falling short of deity and creative power.” BASIL: Whoever says this seems not even to have believed that the deity dwells in us. Yet John says of God: “By this we know that he is in us, by the Spirit whom he has given us.” And the Apostle says: “Do you not know that you are God's temple and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” And again: “In him the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy temple in the Lord; in him you also are built together into a dwelling place of God in the Spirit.” If, then, God is said to dwell in us through the Spirit, how is it not open impiety to say that the Spirit itself has no share in deity? And if we call those who are perfect in virtue gods, and that perfection comes through the Spirit, how can what makes others gods itself fall short of deity? Nor is it pious to say that the Spirit, like human beings, has been honoured with a deity it merely participates in, and that deity does not exist with it by nature. For whoever is deified by grace has a nature that can fall, and sometimes falls away from the better through inattention. This plainly conflicts with the tradition of saving baptism. “Go,” he says, “baptize in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” For baptism is the seal of faith, and faith is assent to deity. One must first believe, and then be sealed with baptism. And our baptism, according to the Lord's tradition, is into the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit. No creature and no servant is ranked with the Father and the Son, since the deity is completed in the Trinity. Everything outside these is a fellow servant, even if some happen to be honoured above others with the very highest ranks. 6. And let me not hear these clever arguments again: EUNOMIUS: “If it is not a creature, then it is either begotten or

unbegotten. But there is one God, without beginning and unbegotten. Nor is it begotten. It remains, then, that it be called a creature and a work.” BASIL: If I had laid it down that all things could be grasped by our knowledge, I might perhaps have been ashamed to confess ignorance. But as it is, countless things are hidden from us. This is true not only of what is stored up for us in the age to come, and not only of what is now in the heavens. Even of what belongs to us in the body we have no clear and indisputable grasp. Take sight, for example. Do we perceive by receiving the images of visible things? Then how is the image of things so vast—the boundless earth, the infinite sea, and even heaven itself—contained in the small measure of our pupil? Or do we send something out from ourselves, which reaches the visible things, and so perceive them? Then what is this, and how large is it, that it is enough to spread out over earth and sea, to cross the space between earth and heaven, and to strike heaven itself, moving so fast that in the same moment we perceive both the body around us and the stars in heaven? And why speak of the rest? Take the very motions of the mind: does the soul by nature create them or beget them? Who could say exactly? What wonder is it, then, if concerning the Holy Spirit too we confess our ignorance without shame, while still rendering it the glory that is indisputably attested of it? For that it is above creation, what is handed down through the Scriptures shows us well enough… (19) The Paris edition reads “unbegotten. But it is not unbegotten.” [?] … The whole passage, “If it is not a creature, then…” [?] … The Regius manuscript [?] reads “ignorance; but since I know that countless… hidden [?].”

…[through him] came into being.” But we are persuaded that the prophetic saying refers not to the Holy Spirit but to this ordinary breath, the wind of the air. The text itself makes this clear. It did not say, “He who created the wind,” but, “He who creates the wind.” Thunder is not something created once for all in some bodily substance. By its nature it is always being made to arise and to dissolve again, at the will of God, to make human beings afraid. The wind is the same: now it arises as the air flows like a river, and then it ceases when what was moving before becomes still, according to the will of him who orders all things for the salvation and preservation of the universe. So through all creation, through thunders and winds and the rest of his handiwork, the Creator is proclaimed. That is why, after saying, “He who establishes the thunder and creates the wind,” it says, “and announces to human beings his Christ.” For as the heavens declare the glory of God to those who can reason from them to the Creator's skill, so also the sounds of thunder and the motions of the winds proclaim their Creator. Perhaps this might also be a prophecy referring to the Lord's incarnation. Then the voice that came from heaven, which God the Father sent forth so as to announce the Christ to human beings through it, seemed like thunder to those who heard it. And the winds that moved and stirred up the sea, then calmed at the Lord's command, clearly also announced his Christ to human beings. And the words “All things came into being through him” in no way show us that the Holy Spirit is created, as though the Spirit were counted among all things. For if the Holy Spirit is one and only, how can what has a unique nature be included among all things? And let no one think that to deny that the Spirit is a creature is to do away with its hypostasis. For a pious mind is careful not to ascribe to the Holy Spirit what the Holy Scriptures pass over in silence, and is convinced that experience of it and exact comprehension are stored up for us in the age to come. Then we will have passed beyond seeing the truth through a mirror and in a riddle, and will be counted worthy of seeing face to face… [?]
